docs.title: axionMultiPhysics
docs.text:
axionMultiPhysics is a finite-element package for electromagnetics, structural mechanics, heat conduction, fluid flow and electrochemistry, with a Python interface, a command line and an interactive field viewer. We built it to design axion dark-matter experiments, which include lumped-element detectors, cavity haloscopes and SRF heterodyne cavities, and it has dedicated tools for them. The solvers themselves are general. Axisymmetric geometries are drawn from polygons, arcs and boolean combinations; 3D geometries from primitives, revolved or extruded profiles and imported CAD (STEP) solids. The same code applies to magnets, superconducting devices, RF structures and resonators in other settings.

What it solves

  • Magnetostatics and magnetoquasistatics: superconducting, resistive and iron-core magnets and shields; fields, inductances and forces, with exact open boundaries.
  • Full-wave electromagnetics: impedances and S-parameters (Touchstone export), radiation losses, eigenmodes and self-resonances.
  • Superconductors: ideal superconductors with flux or current constraints, critical surfaces of NbTi, Nb₃Sn and REBCO, and the HTS critical state.
  • Electrostatics: capacitance matrices.
  • Circuits: networks with the noise of every element, and multiport networks from field solutions.
  • Mechanics and heat: stresses from Lorentz forces and cooldown, and steady heat conduction with a temperature-dependent conductivity.
  • Shape sensitivities and optimization: adjoint gradients, with local, global and derivative-free optimizers.
  • Fluids (beta): Stokes and Navier–Stokes flow, steady and transient, inductionless MHD, and heat transport with natural convection.
  • Electrochemistry (beta): stiff chemical kinetics, reactors, and current distributions in electrolytes.
  • Model documents (beta): one physics-based input format for fluids, heat, electrochemistry and coupled physics, with a physics catalogue, validation, axmp explain, axmp patch and a JSON Schema; planar and axisymmetric documents are meshed with named boundaries, and the meshes can be handed to the fluids and chemistry engines. Solving a model document is not available yet.
  • Export to Geant4 and particle transport (beta): field maps of solved designs, solids and GDML of axisymmetric and 3D designs, and particle transport in axmp-transport, a separate Geant4 program built on request, through the solids and the field map of a design.

Axisymmetric problems run on one machine; 3D problems use MPI.

Walkthroughs

  • Lumped-element detectors: magnets, pickup circuits, and scan sensitivity.
  • dc SQUID readout chains (beta): amplifier noise and detector coupling.
  • Cavity haloscopes (beta): resonant modes, form factors, and sensitivity.
  • SRF heterodyne cavities (beta): pump and signal modes in superconducting radio-frequency cavities.
  • Mechanics and thermal: forces and stresses in a winding, cooldown, and heat loads.
  • Fluids and chemistry (beta): incompressible flow and current distributions in electrolytes.
  • COMSOL export and import: exchange of designs, meshes, and model settings.
  • Meshes of model documents (beta): named boundaries, bounded 2D meshes, and meshes for the fluids and chemistry engines.
  • Field maps, solids and GDML and particle transport (beta): from a solved design to Geant4, with the transport's validation.

Installation · Quick start · API reference

Citing axionMultiPhysics, contact and issues: About

Left: overlap of the pump and signal fields in an SRF heterodyne cavity (beta). Right: von Mises stress in a solenoid winding under its own Lorentz force.

Left: natural convection in a heated square cavity at Ra = 10⁵, temperature and streamlines (beta). Right: primary current distribution on a disk electrode (beta).

docs.title: About
docs.text:
Lumped-element detectors, cavity haloscopes and SRF heterodyne cavities use the axion–photon coupling to search for axion dark matter. Here we outline the goals of axionMultiPhysics and provide citation and contact information.

axionMultiPhysics is introduced in

J. N. Benabou, J. W. Foster, B. R. Safdi, The Price of Discovery: Cost-Optimized Detectors for the GUT-Scale QCD Axion, arXiv:2611.23374 [hep-ph] (2026).

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: The package solves the coupled axion–electromagnetic equations of motion for laboratory experiments that use the axion–photon coupling, and turns the solutions into sensitivity estimates and experimental requirements. Its main focus is lumped-element detectors based on the ABRACADABRA concept (toroidal, solenoidal and CORE geometries); it also covers resonant cavity haloscopes, SRF heterodyne cavities and SQUID readout chains, so that different approaches can be compared on the same footing.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Several modules are beta: they work and are tested, but their interfaces or their validation are not complete. They are the cavity-haloscope, SRF and dc SQUID-chain modules, multi-band and multipole scans, torsional dynamics, the COMSOL import, the fluids, scalar-transport and chemistry modules, the surface-resistance models, and the 3D full-wave features other than current ports. The 3D engine and the fluids module need the MPI source build. Adjoint shape sensitivities cover axisymmetric magnetoquasistatic designs with linear materials. The cost metric compares designs; it is not a construction estimate.

docs.title: Citing axionMultiPhysics
docs.text:
We ask that the paper above be cited in work that uses axionMultiPhysics. The software itself is archived on Zenodo and can be cited with the metadata in CITATION.cff. The DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24298305 always resolves to the newest version; each release also has its own DOI (0.1.0: 10.5281/zenodo.24298306).

docs.title: How axionMultiPhysics was made
docs.text: axionMultiPhysics was developed by its authors with Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding agent in Claude Code, mostly Claude Opus 5.5; most commits in its development history carry a Claude Opus 5.5 co-author trailer. The correctness of the code rests on its checks, not on how it was written: each validated capability is checked against closed-form solutions, manufactured solutions, independent solvers or published results, most of those checks run in the test suite, and modules with less validation evidence are labelled beta. The validation pages document the checks and their tolerances, so that users can judge the results independently of how the code was produced.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text: Lumped-element detectors, cavity haloscopes and SRF heterodyne cavities search for axion dark matter. Here we list the public objects of the axionmultiphysics Python package, grouped by topic.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Every error the package raises is an AxionMultiPhysicsError. Besides its text it has four attributes: where (a JSON pointer into the document, or an empty string), hint (what to change), code (a stable dotted identifier, or an empty string) and details (a dict of structured facts, or None; None also when the details are nested deeper than 64 levels, the details object being level 1, as on the command line and in the MCP reply). The command line prints code and details in its error JSON only when they are not empty (see the command line), and the MCP server's failure reply carries the same four fields.

docs.title: The physics catalogue (beta)
docs.text:
axionmultiphysics.physics(routes=False, type=None) returns the physics catalogue of model documents as a dict, the JSON that axmp physics --json prints (schema axionmultiphysics.physics_catalogue/1): the physics types with their options, condition kinds, sources and quantities, the coupling terms, the reserved instance ids and, with routes=True, the route table and the layer rules. Everything in it is beta, and no route is implemented in this version. The reference page is generated from it.

The codes that the findings about a model document carry are listed in the error codes of the model document, a page generated from the table of codes in the core (axionmultiphysics._core.error_codes() returns it as JSON text). Design.validate(strict=False, all_errors=False) of a model document (one with a top-level physics key) returns its validation report (ok, name, parameters, errors, unavailable, deferred, warnings), raising the first error (with strict, also the first unavailable finding) unless all_errors; axmp.load refuses a model document whose file repeats a key (json.duplicate_key). Design.boundaries(mesh=False, all_errors=False) returns the table of the named boundaries of a model document as axmp boundaries --json prints it (the validation report with symmetry, boundaries and edges added; mesh=True adds faces), raising the first error unless all_errors; axmp.mesh(d, workdir=None, mesher=None) meshes a model document (a Design or a dict) and returns a MeshedModel with symmetry, geometry_order, regions, boundaries, mesh_file, info_file and instance(domain=None), which returns the InstanceMesh of a region or domain name, a list of names or every region: its attributes, remaining_attributes, axis_attributes, master_attribute, region_attribute, the arrays vertices(), elements(), element_attributes(), boundary() and boundary_attributes(), section(name) and face_points(name=None, *, order, attribute=None), the quadrature on the faces of a boundary, a section or one instance attribute (the way to the edges no boundary names and to the axis), with the points, weights and normals as NumPy arrays. Both need the mesher: without one that runs they raise build.requires_mesher; a 3D document, a document on an imported mesh and (for axmp.mesh) a document with no geometry raise route.not_implemented; a failed mesher run is mesh.generation_failed; misuse of an instance mesh (an unknown name, an attribute that is not on it) is a ValueError; an electromagnetic design is refused without a code. An InstanceMesh also has fluids_mesh() (a fluids.Mesh copy of it; MPI builds, else build.requires_fluids) and chem_mesh(order=2) (a chem.TriMesh; MeshedModel.fluids_mesh(domain=None) and MeshedModel.chem_mesh(domain=None, order=2) are shorthands). See meshes of model documents. Design.solve refuses a model document with route.not_implemented, and the electromagnetic-only operations (Design.gradient, Design.optimize, axmp.optimize, axmp.global_optimize, sensitivity.optimize, convert.to_3d, comsol.export_comsol, the model classes of _core) refuse it with model.em_only_operation; both name the operation in details.operation. Design.explain() and Design.patch() read a model document too.

Design.explain(json=False) returns the resolved model of a model document as the text that axmp explain prints, or with json=True as the dict of schema axionmultiphysics.explain/1. It raises AxionMultiPhysicsError for a document that fails validation (the first error) and for an electromagnetic design.

Design.patch(ops) applies an RFC 6902 JSON Patch (a list of operations; paths are RFC 6901 JSON pointers) atomically and returns the design: either every operation applies and the result validates, or AxionMultiPhysicsError is raised and design.doc is unchanged. The keys of the patched document are in sorted order (the order of the keys of a JSON object carries no meaning). An operation that cannot be applied raises with the code patch.operation_failed and where /<index>; a result that does not validate raises the validation's own error. It works on electromagnetic designs too.

docs.title: physics
docs.text:
physics(
    routes: bool = False, type: str | None = None
) -> dict

The physics catalogue of model documents (beta), as axmp physics --json prints it.

The catalogue lists the physics types (their options, condition kinds, sources, quantities per geometry class and what is not implemented), the coupling terms and the reserved instance ids; routes=True adds the route table, one row per combination of physics, couplings, geometry class and study type that an engine of this version solves, with what each row offers and needs, and the rules of this layer. Every entry is beta, and no route is implemented yet (every row has "implemented": False and "status": "not_implemented"). The catalogue is the same in every build. The schema string is axionmultiphysics.physics_catalogue/1.

None

The catalogue: schema, status, types, terms, reserved_ids and, with routes=True, routes and layer_rules.

docs.title: validate
docs.text:
validate(
    strict: bool = False, all_errors: bool = False
) -> dict

Parse and check the design in C++; raises AxionMultiPhysicsError with a hint on problems.

A model document (one with "physics") returns the validation report: ok, name, parameters and the findings errors, unavailable, deferred, warnings. It raises the first error, and with strict the first unavailable finding; all_errors=True returns the report without raising. An electromagnetic design ignores both flags.

docs.title: boundaries
docs.text:
boundaries(
    mesh: bool = False, all_errors: bool = False
) -> dict

The named boundaries of a model document, as axmp boundaries --json prints them (beta).

Validates the document, runs the mesher's resolve_only pass and the full check (the partition rule of every physics, the empty selections, the partial matches, the outputs on resolved boundaries), and returns the validation report with symmetry, boundaries (one row per name: selector, entities, measure, bbox, point, adjacent, used_by) and edges added. mesh=True also meshes the model and adds the number of boundary elements, faces, to every row and edge. Raises AxionMultiPhysicsError with the first error (also build.requires_mesher when the mesher does not run, and mesh.generation_failed); all_errors=True returns the report instead of raising. Needs the mesher; an electromagnetic design is refused.

docs.title: explain
docs.text:
explain(json: bool = False) -> 'str | dict'

The resolved model of a model document (beta), as axmp explain prints it.

Every default is listed and tagged, each physics with its boundary conditions and the form the engine gives them, the coupling terms, the study, the route each group of physics takes and what it needs. Returns the text, or with json=True the dict of schema axionmultiphysics.explain/1. Raises AxionMultiPhysicsError for a document that fails validation (the first error) and for an electromagnetic design.

docs.title: solve
docs.text:
solve(
    workdir: str | Path | None = None,
    order: int = 0,
    verbose: int = 1,
    threads: int | None = None,
    mpi_ranks: int = 1,
    launcher: str | None = None,
    self_force: bool = True,
    force_samples: int = 200,
) -> "Results"

Mesh and solve; returns Results.

workdir defaults to runs/<name>. order overrides mesh.order. 3D designs: mpi_ranks > 1 runs axmp solve --save on that many MPI ranks (launcher: e.g. "srun" or "mpirun"; default: $AXMP_MPI_LAUNCHER, else srun inside a SLURM allocation when srun is on PATH, else mpirun, else mpiexec) and loads the saved solution, so sampling and scenes work as after a single-process solve.

self_force estimates (and, for linear designs, removes) the numerical self-force of each powered azimuthal winding, at the price of one extra linear solve per such winding (axisymmetric designs only).

force_samples is the number of samples per body in forces.distributions. The merge that produces them preserves the integral, so the net forces do not depend on it; it only sets how finely the load is resolved and how big results.json gets (about 160 bytes per sample per body). 0 keeps the net forces and the closure check but writes no arrays.

docs.title: export_gdml
docs.text:
export_gdml(
    path: str | Path,
    composition: dict,
    *,
    solids: str | Path | None = None,
    chord_tol_m: float | None = None,
    workdir: str | Path | None = None,
    mesher: str | Path | None = None,
) -> dict

Writes the geometry of an axisymmetric or 3D electromagnetic design as GDML for particle transport (beta).

The route is the design's mesher input (the one axmp mesh writes), axmp-mesher --export-regions on it (the exact partition of the model: its regions, the background air included, with their curves) and axionmultiphysics.solids.from_partition() on that partition. Returns the solids document (axionmultiphysics.solids/1) and writes the GDML at path and, when solids is a path, the document as solids.json there.

composition maps each material name the regions use to a particle block (nist, or elements and by; optional mean_excitation_eV, state, T_K, pressure_Pa) with an optional density (kg/m3). A region takes its design material, the background region the material named air. A material's density is the design's (as the electromagnetic parser resolves it: the built-in iron, copper and nb values, expressions evaluated) when it has one, else the block's density; two different positive values are particle.composition_invalid, none particle.density_missing, and a used material without a block particle.composition_missing. Blocks of materials no region uses are ignored.

For a 3D design the mesher input is the 3D engine's (mesh3d_in.json, made by the same library function in every build, without running the engine: each rank of a parallel program exports on its own), the partition the mesher's 3D one (one triangulation of every face, to the chord tolerance) and the solids are tessellated; chord_tol_m then goes to the mesher (default: min(1 mm, 1e-4 x the diagonal of the geometry)). A design reduced by symmetry planes (mesh.symmetry) is refused.

chord_tol_m is the conversion's chord tolerance. workdir, when given, keeps regions_in.json (the mesher input) and regions.json (the partition); without it nothing is left behind. mesher is the program (default: $AXMP_MESHER, else the one of the package). Refused: a model document (model.em_only_operation); a 3D design with mesh.symmetry, an imported mesh (mesh.file) and a mesher without the export mode (particle.partition_unavailable); a mesher that cannot be run or loaded (build.requires_mesher, with the loader's message); a planar design (particle.planar_not_offered); a failed mesher run (mesh.generation_failed, the last lines of the mesher's log in the hint; with workdir the log is kept there as regions_mesher.log). Nothing is written then.

forces: dict

Lorentz / Maxwell forces.

Per winding: Fz_N and radial_force_per_radian_N (the hoop load); for a powered azimuthal winding also Fz_self_N (the numerical self-force, exactly zero in theory, so the error bar on Fz_N) and Fz_excluding_self_N (the force from all other sources -- the number to quote for a linear design). Per body: superconductor:<name> / iron:<name> Maxwell pressure forces. closure is the Newton's-third-law sum over all bodies, which must vanish. distributions holds the distributed load of each body; plot it with axionmultiphysics.plots.force_distribution().

docs.title: port_capacitance property
docs.text:
port_capacitance: dict

Readout-gap capacitance of a poloidal (port) pickup: C_gap_F (with fringing), C_gap_port_region_F (gap region only, no fringing) and the self-resonance estimates.

Neither capacitance is a proven bound on the other: the rigorous relation, exact for the discrete problems, is checks.dirichlet_bound. self_resonance_Hz = 1/(2 pi sqrt(L_p C_gap)) is an estimate of the first self-resonance, not a bound.

docs.text:

Eigenmodes of a cavity design (design section cavity) as flat rows sorted by frequency: family ("TE"/"TM"; "3D" for 3D designs), index (within the family), f_Hz, C (B0 at the reference point), C_rms, V_m3, G_ohm (geometry factor Q R_s of all walls), Q_wall, Q_dielectric, Q0, T_over_Q_K, residual_true, energy_fraction, walls (per body: G_ohm, Rs_ohm, Q, P_frac). Missing quantities are None. Empty for designs without a cavity section.

docs.title: cavity_mode_field
docs.text:
cavity_mode_field(
    i=0, family: str | None = None, *, subdiv: int = 2
) -> dict

Fields of a cavity eigenmode on the cavity mesh (2D designs with a cavity section).

i indexes cavity_modes() (all families, sorted by frequency); with family ("TE"/"TM") it is the index within that family (row["index"]); a row of cavity_modes() also works. Returns numpy arrays over a lattice of points per cavity element (subdiv = 2: vertices and edge midpoints; points on element edges repeat with each element's value): r, z [m], tris (n, 3) sub-triangles, E_r, E_phi, E_z, H_r, H_phi, H_z, Emag, Hmag, flux, eps_r, mu_r, elem (element number), and mode (f_Hz, C, G_ohm, Q0, ... of the row).

Normalization: int eps_r |E|^2 dV = 1 over the cavity (E in m^-3/2, the normalization of the form factor); H is the matching physical field, so int mu_r |H|^2 dV = eps0/mu0 = 1/Z0^2 at resonance. The arrays are real amplitudes: the complex fields are E_c = i E, H_c = H (e^{-i omega t}, i.e. E(t) = E sin(omega t), H(t) = H cos(omega t)). TM modes have (E_r, E_z, H_phi), TE modes (E_phi, H_r, H_z); the other components are zero. The sign is fixed so that the largest E component at the point of largest |E| is positive (a convention: for modes whose |E| maxima are mirror images with opposite signs, e.g. TM011, it may differ between meshes). flux = r H_phi (TM; E field lines are its contours) or r E_phi/omega (TE; H field lines).

docs.text:
sensitivities(
    params: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    objectives: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    method: str = "adjoint",
    step: float = 0.0001,
    steps: dict | None = None,
    benchmark: str = "",

) -> dict

Derivatives of the figures of merit with respect to design parameters.

params defaults to every entry of the design's parameters, objectives to Psi, L_p, W_mag, F and the cost of the first benchmark (axionmultiphysics.objectives() lists them all; cost quantities accept a benchmark, e.g. "cost:optimistic"). method: "adjoint" (discrete adjoint on a morphed mesh, the default), "fd_morph" (central differences with mesh morphing) or "fd_remesh" (central differences with a new mesh per evaluation; the only method for nonlinear iron or for parameters that change the mesh topology). step is the relative finite-difference step, steps gives absolute per-parameter overrides.

docs.title: reach
docs.text:
reach(
    benchmark: str = "optimistic",
    amplitude: str = "required",
    **kw,
) -> dict

Expected 95% reach g_95(m_a) of this design for a noise benchmark. amplitude='required': field scaled so that F = F_req (reaches the QCD target); 'as_designed': the ampere-turns given in the design. Extra keywords go to scan.reach.

docs.title: readout
docs.text:
readout(
    f_Hz: float | None = None,
    benchmark: str | dict | None = None,
    amplitude: str = "as_designed",
    model: str = "mqs",
    pickup_Q: float | None = None,
    R_loss_ohm: float | None = None,
    parasitic: bool = False,
    analyze: bool = True,
    **kw,
) -> dict

Readout-circuit analysis of this solved design.

Builds a DMRadio-style network -- pickup in series with a tuning capacitor, the SQUID input coil and the leads -- from this design's Psi, L_p and losses, tunes it to f_Hz (default: the middle of the design's scan band in log frequency) and returns the analysis: resonance, loaded Q, referred T_eff, the amplifier coupling xi, the signal flux into the SQUID, the Johnson/amplifier noise budget, the bandwidths and the equivalent optimal-scan inputs (Psi, L_eff, Q, T, eta_A).

model="mqs": Z_p = R_loss - i omega L_p with R_loss from R_loss_ohm, from pickup_Q, or from the design's RF surface losses. model="fullwave": Z_p(omega) interpolated from results["fullwave"]["sweep"]. benchmark sets T_K and eta_A from scan.BENCHMARKS (and, when no loss data and no pickup_Q are available, the pickup Q too). amplitude="required" scales Psi so that F = F_req for that benchmark. parasitic=True puts this design's readout-port gap capacitance (pickup/port_capacitance/C_gap_F, only the gap's share of the distributed capacitance) across the pickup, so that the self-resonance it implies is part of the circuit. Extra keywords go to axionmultiphysics.circuit.series_readout() (L_in_H, R_in_ohm, lead_length_m, L_per_m, R_per_m, tan_delta, M_H, xi, ...). The returned dict carries the live Readout under "readout"; it holds complex impedances, so it is not JSON-serialisable.

docs.title: draw_readout
docs.text:
draw_readout(annotate: bool = True, **kw)

Effective-circuit schematic of this design's readout: the network that readout() builds (same keywords: f_Hz, benchmark, model, pickup_Q, parasitic, L_in_H, ...), drawn by axionmultiphysics.circuit.Readout.draw() with the values at f_Hz. Needs schemdraw (axionmultiphysics[draw]).

docs.title: export_field_map
docs.text:
export_field_map(
    path: str | Path,
    *,
    regions: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    tol: float = 0.0001,
    merge: bool = True,
    track_volumes: Sequence[dict] | None = None,
    iterate_on_track_volumes: bool = False,
    outside: str = "refuse",
    max_patch_MB: float = 512.0,
    max_total_MB: float = 2048.0,
)

Field map of the static field for particle transport (beta; axionmultiphysics.fieldmap, docs/guides/field_maps.md): one patch per region (kind 1 here, kind 3 for 3D results), each sampling the region's recovered field B* on its own grid and refined until the RMS error of its chord integrals, relative to max(int |B*| dl, 0.1 L_c B_patch), meets tol (or a tenth of the FE indicator, whichever is larger).

regions: the regions to map (default: every region but ideal superconductors, where B = 0); merge: adjacent regions with the same constitutive law and no curve between them share a patch; a closed curve (superconducting sheet or thin magnetic layer) splits its region into one patch per side, and an open one is refused. track_volumes: boxes {"name", "r": [lo, hi], "z": [lo, hi]} (3D: "x", "y", "z") whose own chord families are reported, and iterated on with iterate_on_track_volumes. outside: what the evaluator does outside a patch's box ("refuse" or "zero"). max_patch_MB, max_total_MB: caps (MB = 2^20 bytes). Writes the directory path and returns fieldmap.load(path); refusals write nothing.

docs.title: torsion
docs.text:
torsion(
    nmodes: int = 0,
    load=None,
    freqs_Hz=None,
    eta: float = 0.0001,
    shapes: bool = False,
    regions: dict | None = None,
    dofs: bool = False,
    lanczos_extra: int = 24,
    verbose: int = 0,
    loads: list | None = None,
    band: dict | None = None,
    solver: dict | None = None,
    mesh_check: str = "error",
) -> dict

Axisymmetric m = 0 torsional modal / harmonic analysis (beta; physics: docs/physics/mechanics_thermal.md and docs/physics/torsion_highfreq.md; validation: docs/validation/torsion.md and docs/validation/torsion_highfreq.md).

Loads (they add up): - load: one azimuthal body-force value per degree of freedom of the space (use dofs=True once to get dof_r, dof_z); the FEM integrates its P_p interpolant, and the response reports what was applied (load.force_N, load.torque_N_m); - loads: a list of named loads, integrated exactly at quadrature points: {"region": R, "g_N_m3": v} (body force in region R), {"surface": {"on": R, "from": S or "vacuum"}, "traction_Pa": v} (azimuthal traction on the faces R shares with S), {"curve": C, "traction_Pa": v} (on a zero-thickness curve); v is a number, an expression in r and z [m] (e.g. "exp(-z^2/(2*0.005^2))") or one value per DOF. Expressions use standard precedence: exp(-z^2/(2*0.005^2)) is a Gaussian. Check loads.total.force_N against the load you meant. With freqs_Hz, or band = {"f_Hz": [f0, f1], "n": N, "length_m": L} (N odd; length_m optional), the response returns the generalised mobility Y = -i omega q of the conjugate pair (load scale, q = int g u_phi dV + int tau u_phi dA), time dependence e^{-i omega t}; S_q = 4 kB T Re[Y]/omega^2. harmonic.band holds the band mean of Re Y, its quadrature uncertainty, a ripple diagnostic and, with length_m, a conservative scale of the finite-length deviation (edge_estimate). Single frequencies are not certified by the mesh guard (it is calibrated on band means). solver = {"backend": "auto"|"eigen"|"strumpack", "parallel_frequencies": p | "auto"}. mesh_check ("error", "warn", "off") guards the elements per shear wavelength at the highest frequency (harmonic.resolution).

docs.title: torsion_band
docs.text:
torsion_band(
    f_min: float,
    f_max: float,
    loads=None,
    load=None,
    eta: float = 0.001,
    n: int = 201,
    solver: dict | None = None,
    mesh_check: str = "error",
    regions: dict | None = None,
    verbose: int = 0,
    length_m: float | None = None,
) -> dict

Band-averaged torsional mobility over [f_min, f_max] (n frequencies, n odd): harmonic.band holds the mean of Re Y, its quadrature uncertainty, a ripple diagnostic (ripple_sem) and, with length_m (the structure's axial length), edge_estimate, a conservative scale of how far the band mean of the finite structure may sit from a smooth value (docs/physics/torsion_highfreq.md). The default solver is serial STRUMPACK (serial Eigen SparseLU in a build without STRUMPACK): robust in memory and never far from the fastest choice. solver={"parallel_frequencies": "auto"} opts in to the measured choice between concurrent Eigen solves and serial STRUMPACK (faster on thin walls; it costs one STRUMPACK and possibly one Eigen probe solve).

docs.title: global_optimize
docs.text:
global_optimize(
    design,
    objective: Any = "cost",
    params: dict | None = None,
    *,
    bounds: dict | None = None,
    constraints: Iterable = (),
    sense: str = "min",
    log: Sequence[str] = (),
    seed: int | None = 0,
    popsize: int = 15,
    maxiter: int = 50,
    tol: float = 0.01,
    atol: float = 0.0,
    mutation: Any = (0.5, 1.0),
    recombination: float = 0.7,
    strategy: str = "best1bin",
    init: Any = "latinhypercube",
    x0: dict | None = None,
    workers: Any = 1,
    threads: int = 1,
    timeout: float | None = None,
    max_time: float | None = None,
    polish: Any = True,
    polish_max_iter: int = 30,
    polish_maxfev: int = 200,
    benchmark: str = "",
    amplitude: str | None = "auto",
    amplitude_tol: float = 1e-06,
    amplitude_max_solves: int = 16,
    workdir: str | Path | None = None,
    order: int = 0,
    keep_runs: bool = False,
    precheck: Callable | None = None,
    verbose: int = 1,
    callback: Callable | None = None,
) -> dict

Global minimization (or maximization) of a figure of merit by differential evolution.

params (or its alias bounds; not both) maps parameter names to (low, high) or (low, high, "log"); log lists parameters searched in log space (use it for sizes and ratios spanning decades). objective is a quantity name (axionmultiphysics.objectives(), e.g. "cost", "cost_optimal:conservative", "g_factor") or a picklable callable f(results) -> float (importable by name in a worker when workers > 1 or a map is given). constraints holds {"quantity": "sc_surface_at_req", "type": "<=", "value": 0.093} entries (or 3-tuples); they are enforced by the feasibility rule, not by a penalty weight. values are keyed by the quantity name; a callable by its __name__ ("custom" without one), suffixed #2, #3 ... when that key is already taken (two lambdas, or a callable named like a quantity). A feasible objective must have |f| < 1e99 (larger values are failed points: rescale).

DE settings are scipy's: the population has max(5, popsize * len(params)) members (rounded up to a power of 2 for init="sobol"; an init array is given in parameter units, one row per member, inside the bounds), at most maxiter generations after the initial one. The search stops when the whole population is feasible and std(f) <= atol + tol * |mean(f)| (scipy >= 1.12; older scipy runs all maxiter generations). It is deterministic for a given seed: every evaluation (serial, pool or map) and the polish run on threads OpenMP threads (default 1; the calling process is set to it and restored on return), so that the solver's parallel sums do not depend on the thread count. workers > 1 evaluates each generation on a process pool (-1: the CPUs this process may use, divided by threads); a callable workers(fn, tasks) -> records (a map) distributes evaluations elsewhere, e.g. a SLURM array. Scripts that use a process pool must guard their entry point with if __name__ == "__main__":.

Failure handling. A shape that fails to mesh or solve is an infeasible point. With a process pool (workers > 1) also: an evaluation slower than timeout [s] (killed when still running timeout s after submission, which includes a worker's start-up after a restart, then the pool is restarted and the other running points are re-run; a finished one whose own run time exceeds timeout is charged too) and a worker that dies (the points running with it are re-run one at a time, so the crash is charged to the point that caused it). In serial mode (workers=1) timeout is ignored (with a warning) and a hard crash of the solver ends the run. Nothing is saved before the run returns. An error of the configuration (an unknown benchmark, cost_optimal on an iron design, a nonlinear design without an amplitude parameter, NI optimized while it is the amplitude, a callable that cannot be loaded in a worker, ...) is raised as ValueError at the first evaluation that shows it, instead of failing every point.

max_time [s] is checked after every generation (not inside one, nor during the initial population): the search then stops, the polish is skipped if the time is exhausted, the Powell polish stops when it is, and the adjoint polish (which cannot be interrupted; at most polish_max_iter iterations) is replaced by Powell unless 7 (polish_max_iter + 1) evaluations of the DE's mean duration fit in the remaining time (an iteration takes several solves). max_time is thus a soft bound: the last generation, a Powell evaluation, or an adjoint polish that needs more solves than this estimate can overrun it. callback(generation, best_record) returning True stops the search too.

precheck(parameters) rejects a point before it is meshed: a returned string (the reason, also an empty one), False (also numpy.False_) or a raised exception rejects it, None or True (also numpy.True_) accepts it; any other return value is an error. Use it for cheap geometric rules (wall thickness, corner radii). polish="adjoint" cannot apply it and is refused with a precheck.

Requirement quantities (cost, cost_optimal, W_at_req, sc_surface_at_req, ...) are read at F = F_req: by the solver's exact rescaling for linear designs, as by axionmultiphysics.optimize(); when the rescaling is not exact (nonlinear iron, or fixed sources such as a background field) the parameter amplitude (default "NI") is solved for F = F_req of the objective's benchmark to amplitude_tol (log-secant, at most amplitude_max_solves solves), and all requirement quantities must then refer to that benchmark. A nonlinear solve whose Newton iteration did not converge is a failed point. Known limitation: the amplitude at which the other quantities are read differs by case. When the root runs (a requirement quantity or any callable is asked for on a nonlinear design or one with fixed sources), every quantity and callable -- also B_peak, W_mag, sc_surface_peak -- is read at the root amplitude; on a linear design without fixed sources, non-requirement quantities and callables see the design's own NI. A constraint such as ("B_peak", "<=", 6) therefore means different things in the two cases; use the *_at_req quantities for limits at the operating point. A callable on a nonlinear design needs the amplitude parameter and costs the ~3 solves of the root.

polish: True/"auto" refines the best point with the adjoint-gradient optimizer when the design is linear without fixed sources (no amplitude root), the objective and constraints are named quantities, no precheck is given and order is 0, else with bounded Powell; "adjoint" (falling back to Powell if the adjoint optimizer fails or the point needed the amplitude root), "powell" or False choose. The polished point replaces the DE point only if it is feasible and better.

Returns the structure of axionmultiphysics.optimize() (parameters, values, caps, constraints, design, history of every evaluation with stage, generation, energy and feasible), plus feasible, de (generations, evaluations, convergence, scipy's own message), de_best, polish and found_by. converged is the DE convergence test above and message says how the search ended. evaluations is len(history) (DE and Powell points, adjoint iterates, precheck rejections); solves counts the FE solves (one per evaluated point, plus the amplitude-root and adjoint-polish solves). The default workdir is a new directory per run under runs/<design>__global/.

docs.title: reach
docs.text:
reach(
    Psi_SI: float,
    L_H: float,
    benchmark: str | dict = "optimistic",
    live_time_yr: float = 3.0,
    f_min: float = 120900.0,
    f_max: float = 1000000.0,
    allocation: str = "target",
    n: int = 200,
    model: str = "DFSZ",
    C_gamma: float = 1.77,
    Q_axion: float = 680000.0,
    Theta: float = 2.71,
    rho: float = 0.3,
) -> dict

Expected 95% upper-limit reach g_95(m_a) of a detector (Psi [H T m^2], L_p [H]) for a noise benchmark, with the optimal resonant scan over [f_min, f_max] in the live time. The default band, live time and model (DFSZ over 0.5-4.1 neV in 3 years) and the benchmarks are illustrative: set them for your study. allocation: 'target' (time distributed to follow the QCD line) or 'log_uniform'.

The result carries a "band" dict that echoes what was scanned -- mass and frequency range, number of mass points, allocation, live time, the benchmark (Q, T, eta_A), the detector (Psi, L, F) and the scan conventions (Q_axion, Theta, rho, v0, vobs, the QCD line) -- so that an output document is self-describing.

benchmark["eta_A"] may also be a callable eta_A(f_Hz), e.g. an axionmultiphysics.squid.Chain (squid.benchmark(chain, Q, T_K)). The scan then runs reach_dispersive() with constant Psi, L, Q, T and the frequency-dependent eta_A. That route also applies reach_dispersive's local-validity guards (noise bandwidth < 0.1 f, slow variation), which the scalar route does not, so a very low Q raises there; and its band entries for Q, T, eta_A, L, Psi are [f_min, f_max] endpoint values rather than scalars.

docs.title: reach_fullwave
docs.text:
reach_fullwave(
    results,
    benchmark: str | dict = "optimistic",
    *,
    amplitude: str = "as_designed",
    T_K: float | None = None,
    eta_A: float | None = None,
    Q_floor: float | None = None,
    compare_mqs: bool = True,
    T_radiation_K: float | None = None,
    **kw,
) -> dict

Local beyond-MQS reach with the series-tuned slope inductance.

Independent resistances add: R_total=R_rad+R_material+omega*L_p/Q_other. The Q_floor argument (or the benchmark's Q) is the intrinsic MQS Q_other, referenced to the static L_p; it is not a minimum-Q ceiling. The MQS comparison retains material and intrinsic losses and removes radiation. Material/intrinsic loss is at T_K. Radiation uses T_radiation_K; omitting it explicitly assumes the same bath temperature and records that assumption. Both the tabulated slope and local noise bandwidth must pass the guards in reach_dispersive. Requested bands must lie in the contiguous positive-L sweep. For broad or rapidly dispersive response use finite_band with a tuned circuit.

The sweep's R_ohm holds the surface loss R_loss that the engines compute from the conductors' rf blocks (2D and 3D), so Q_other must exclude that loss: a benchmark Q that stands for the total intrinsic Q counts the conductor loss twice. When every row carries the exact tuned-pole L_eff_H (3D designs whose conductors are meshed as volumes: from dZ/domega), the full-wave scan takes L_eff from a cubic Hermite interpolant of L with those exact slopes, which must agree with the linear interpolation of the rows' L_eff within 5 % (else the rows are too sparse and the reach refuses), instead of L + 0.5 dL/dln(f) of the interpolated L (which needs four rows and spline/PCHIP agreement within 5 %). The MQS comparison always uses L_p.

docs.title: finite_band
docs.text:
finite_band(
    readout,
    f_min_Hz: float,
    f_max_Hz: float,
    *,
    n_settings: int = 40,
    n_targets: int = 60,
    xi_factors: Sequence[float] = (1.0,),
    match_xi: bool = True,
    model: str = "DFSZ",
    C_gamma: float = 1.77,
    Theta: float = 2.71,
    rho: float = 0.3,
    Q_axion: float | None = None,
    stat: str = "weak",
    n_v: int = 96,
    half_widths: float = 60.0,
    decades: float = 3.0,
    points_per_decade: float = 48.0,
    band_points: int = 200,
    band_margin: float = 4.0,
    reduced: bool = True,
    reduced_R_exp: float = 0.0,
    narrow_line: bool = True,
    local_schedule: bool = True,
    convergence: bool = False,
    live_time_yr: float | None = None,
) -> dict

Plan a scan with the exact circuit noise N_V(omega) instead of the reduced pole.

Driven by axionmultiphysics.circuit: for each setting -- a tuning capacitance (hence an omega_0) and a coupling xi -- the readout network is tuned, N_V(omega) is tabulated exactly (noise_curve()), and the C++ kernel

``K_j(m) = (1/2pi) int domega h(S_Va(omega)/N_{V,j}(omega))``   [1/s]

is built for every target mass. The minimum-total-time schedule is the LP, and the reach follows from sum_j t_j K_j(m) = Theta. The pickup's Psi is taken from the readout at each tuning, so a frequency-dependent Psi(omega) is used if the readout has one.

With reduced=True the same settings are also evaluated through the single-pole reduction of each setting (L_eff, Q, T_eff, eta_A_eff, xi), which is what the rest of the package uses; comparison then quantifies the error of that reduction. reduced_R_exp gives the reduced pole a power-law resistance R(omega) = R_0 (omega/omega_0)^{R_exp} within a tuning (0 = constant, 1/2 for a normal-metal skin effect, 2 for a superconductor), which is the one piece of dispersion the single pole can carry. narrow_line=True adds the narrow-line kernel, evaluated with the exact N_V(omega_a). convergence=True repeats the kernel with half the N_V grid density and half the line nodes, so the numerical error of the exact kernel is reported rather than assumed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default readout

an axionmultiphysics.circuit.Readout with a tuning capacitor (tuner) -- it is tuned in place, setting by setting, and left at the last setting -- or a callable f0_Hz -> Readout that builds the network for each tuning. The factory form is the one to use when the network itself depends on the tuning (a surface resistance quoted at the operating point, a full-wave Z_p(omega) and Psi(omega), a different input coil per octave); Psi(omega) is read from the first instance, the pickup being the same.

required n_settings int

n_settings log-spaced tunings over [f_min, f_max] times one setting per entry of xi_factors (multiples of xi_opt; match_xi rescales M accordingly).

40 xi_factors Sequence[float]

See n_settings.

(1.0,) n_targets int

log-spaced target masses over the same band; the LP covers these exactly and the returned reach is evaluated on them.

60 live_time_yr float | None

if given, the LP schedule is also reported rescaled to this live time (coverage_at_live_time = the Theta reached per target, in units of Theta).

None Notes

local_schedule=True also discretises the local optimal-scan dwell density onto the settings and scores it with the exact kernel: a plan made from the Lorentzian scan rate covers at ~Theta only while the sensitivity band is narrow.

Returns a dict with band (the echo), settings, targets, K_per_s, schedule, reach, and -- when asked for -- reduced/narrow_line/ local_schedule/convergence and comparison.

docs.text:
series_readout(
    L_p_H: float | None = None,
    *,
    Z_p: ZFunc | None = None,
    Psi_SI: float | Callable[[float], float] = 0.0,
    f_Hz: float = 120900.0,
    Q: float | None = None,
    R_loss_ohm: float = 0.0,
    T_K: float = 0.02,
    C_F: float | None = None,
    tan_delta: float = 0.0,
    T_C_K: float | None = None,
    C_par_F: float = 0.0,
    tan_delta_par: float = 0.0,
    T_par_K: float | None = None,
    L_in_H: float = 0.0,
    R_in_ohm: float = 0.0,
    T_in_K: float | None = None,
    L_lead_H: float = 0.0,
    R_lead_ohm: float = 0.0,
    T_lead_K: float | None = None,
    lead_length_m: float = 0.0,
    L_per_m: float = 0.0,
    R_per_m: float = 0.0,
    M_H: float | None = None,
    k_in: float | None = None,
    L_squid_H: float = 0.0,
    eta_A: float = 1.0,
    xi: float | None = None,
    S_Phi: float | None = None,
    transformer_ratio: float | None = None,
    L_1_H: float = 0.0,
    L_2_H: float = 0.0,
    k_T: float = 1.0,
    R_2_ohm: float = 0.0,
    T_2_K: float | None = None,
    label: str | None = None,
) -> Readout

DMRadio-style readout: pickup in series with a tuning capacitor and the SQUID input coil.

Plain series topology (the default):

gnd -[ pickup: EMF, Z_p ]- a -[ L_lead ]- b -[ R_lead ]- c
    -[ C (tan_delta) ]- d -[ R_in ]- e -[ L_in ]- gnd          (M couples L_in -> SQUID)

With transformer_ratio an ideal transformer closes the resonant loop and the input coil (plus R_2_ohm) sits on its secondary; with L_1_H and L_2_H a real flux transformer (two inductors coupled by k_T) does the same job with finite inductance and leakage.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default L_p_H float | None

the pickup, either as an inductance (Z_p = R_loss - i omega L_p, R_loss from R_loss_ohm or from Q at f_Hz) or as a callable Z_p(omega) -- e.g. pickup_impedance() built from a solved design's full-wave sweep. With Z_p the pickup inductance used for the participation ratio is -Im Z_p(2 pi f_Hz)/omega unless L_p_H is also given.

None Z_p ZFunc | None

See L_p_H.

None Psi_SI float | Callable[[float], float]

the design's signal coupling [T H m^2]; the EMF amplitude is omega kappa_a Psi_SI. A callable Psi_SI(omega) -- e.g. pickup_coupling() built from the design's full-wave sweep -- makes the coupling frequency dependent.

0.0 C_F float | None

the tuning capacitance; None (default) tunes it to resonate at f_Hz.

None C_par_F float

a parasitic capacitance across the pickup terminals -- e.g. the solver's results["pickup"]["port_capacitance"]["C_gap_F"], which sets the self-resonance f_SR = 1/(2 pi sqrt(L_p C_gap)). The loop is then not a plain series chain, and the reduction diagnostics (backaction_transfer_ratio, react_resid) show it.

0.0 L_lead_H float

the leads: either L_lead_H/R_lead_ohm, or lead_length_m with L_per_m [H/m] and R_per_m [ohm/m].

0.0 R_lead_ohm float

See L_lead_H.

0.0 lead_length_m float

See L_lead_H.

0.0 L_per_m float

See L_lead_H.

0.0 R_per_m float

See L_lead_H.

0.0 T_K float

temperatures: T_K is the default for every dissipative element; T_C_K, T_in_K, T_lead_K and T_2_K override it per element (the referred T_eff then obeys T_eff/Q = sum_k T_k/Q_k).

0.02 T_C_K float | None

See T_K.

None T_in_K float | None

See T_K.

None T_lead_K float | None

See T_K.

None T_2_K float | None

See T_K.

None M_H float | None

SQUID coupling: M_H directly; or k_in with L_squid_H (M = k sqrt(L_in L_squid)); or neither, in which case M is derived from xi (default: xi_opt at the resonance, which is what the optimal scan assumes). S_Phi [Wb^2 s] fixes the amplifier's flux noise; left out, it is derived from xi with the reference M = L_in (k = 1 to a SQUID of the input coil's inductance), or M = L_eff when there is no input coil. Only the absolute flux in Wb depends on that reference; Q, T_eff, xi, G-bar, N_V and the reach do not.

None k_in float | None

See M_H.

None L_squid_H float

See M_H.

0.0 S_Phi float | None

See M_H.

None

Resonant angular frequency: the omega nearest the guess where Im Z_eff = 0.

docs.title: tune
docs.text:
tune(
    f_Hz: float,
    branch: str | None = None,
    span: float = 1000000.0,
) -> float

Set the tuning capacitor so that the loop resonates at f_Hz; returns C [F].

The start value is the closed form C = -1/(omega X_rest) with X_rest the loop reactance with the capacitor shorted; bisection on Im Z_eff(2 pi f) = 0 then makes it exact for any network (a transformer-coupled secondary, a frequency-dependent Z_p, ...).

docs.title: equivalent
docs.text:
equivalent(
    omega0: float | None = None,
    f_Hz: float | None = None,
    dlog: float = 1e-05,
    corr_tol: float = 0.01,
) -> dict

Reduce the network to the single-pole detector the optimal scan assumes.

Definitions (all exact for the series topology):

  • omega0 : Im Z_eff(omega0) = 0
  • R_eff : Re Z_eff(omega0)
  • L_eff : |dIm Z_eff/domega|/2 at omega0 (the reactance-slope inductance; = L_p + L_in + L_lead for a series loop)
  • Q_loaded : omega0 L_eff/R_eff
  • n_eff : from sum_k |H_k/H_s|^2 R_k (2 n_k + 1) = R_eff (2 n_eff + 1), so the referred thermal noise is matched exactly; T_eff/Q = sum_k T_k/Q_k classically
  • xi : 2 R_eff S_Phi/(hbar omega0 |M_eff|^2)
  • participation: L_p/L_eff, the amplitude factor; the scan rate carries its square

With a correlated SQUID (S_PhiJ != 0) the noise is reduced by completing the square; correlated_reduction_resid compares that pole with the exact N_V at the noise-doubling points and the call raises above corr_tol.

react_resid, R_noise_over_R_eff, backaction_transfer_ratio and reciprocity_resid are the diagnostics that say how good the reduction is: the first should be ~0, the next two ~1, the last ~0. R_noise_over_R_eff is the Nyquist identity referred with the pickup current (the flux referral is not an identity); reciprocity_resid is the asymmetry of the solved branch transfer matrix, and matrix_symmetry_resid the tautological assembled-matrix one. port_coupling is Q1/sqrt(1 + Q1^2) with Q1 = coupling_Q1, not 1.

docs.title: signal
docs.text:
signal(
    omega: float,
    g_GeV: float = 1e-19,
    rho_GeV_cm3: float = 0.3,
) -> dict

Signal amplitudes at omega for an axion of coupling g.

The pickup EMF amplitude is |V| = omega kappa_a Psi_SI (with Phi_a = kappa_a Psi_SI). Returns the EMF, the pickup current, the flux into the SQUID in Wb and in Phi_0, and two ratios: Phi_SQUID_per_kappa_Wb_H and flux_gain = |Phi_SQ|/Phi_a. flux_gain is a resonant gain, not an efficiency: on resonance it is ~ Q M/L and is routinely much larger than 1. The dc flux-transfer efficiency of a non-resonant superconducting loop is instead M/(L_p + L_in), which flux_transformer_circuit() exercises.

docs.title: noise_curve
docs.text:
noise_curve(
    omega0: float | None = None,
    *,
    half_widths: float = 60.0,
    decades: float = 3.0,
    points_per_decade: float = 48.0,
    extra_omega: Sequence[float] | None = None,
    omega: Sequence[float] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, ndarray | float]

The exact N_V(omega) of this setting tabulated for the finite-band kernel.

The finite-band kernel needs N_V(omega) of each setting (one tuning capacitance, one coupling), not the single-pole reduction of it; this returns it on a grid that the C++ kernel_row_noise interpolates log-log. The grid is symmetric in the detuning,

``omega = omega0`` and ``omega0 +- hw x``,  ``x`` geometric over
``[10^-decades, half_widths]`` at ``points_per_decade`` points per decade,

with hw half the noise-doubling width of the equivalent pole, so it resolves the resonance (where N_V is flat, so the x < 10^-decades gap costs nothing) and the |Z|^2 ~ (2 L domega)^2 wings (where N_V is a power law, hence exact in log-log). half_widths = 60 covers the window the discrete sums use (+-40 half-widths truncate below 1e-5). The interpolation error of N_V is second order in the step, ~(ln 10/ppd)^2/8, so 48 points per decade keeps K (which goes as 1/N_V^2) accurate to a few times 10^-4; halve points_per_decade to check.

extra_omega merges extra frequencies into the grid. Use it for structure that does not scale with the detuning -- above all a self-resonance of Z_p (a pole at a fixed frequency), which a grid centred on omega_0 resolves only by accident.

Pass omega= to use your own grid instead. Returns omega_rad_s, f_Hz, N_V_V2_s and its components (thermal, backaction, imprecision, correlation), plus omega0_rad_s, f0_Hz and N_V_at_omega0_V2_s.

docs.title: kernel
docs.text:
kernel(
    omega0: float | None = None,
    g_GeV: float = 1e-19,
    Q_axion: float = 680000.0,
    rho_GeV_cm3: float = 0.3,
    Theta: float = 2.71,
) -> dict

Narrow-line matched-filter kernel at resonance, in SI:

K = (pi/8) Q_a omega_a^3 Phi_a^4/N_V(omega_a)^2    [1/s]

(Phi_a in Wb, N_V in V^2 s; no hbar appears because Wb^4 s^-3/(V^2 s)^2 = s^-1). K is the Asimov TS gained per second of dwell at coupling g for an axion on resonance, and dwell_for_Theta_s = Theta/K is the time one tuning needs for a 95% limit there. Unlike the scan rate, K does not involve L: a bigger total inductance narrows the band without changing the on-resonance SNR.

docs.text:
kappa_g2_scan(f_Hz, Q: float, T_K: float)

Scan-optimal global coupling: kappa_g^2 = (1/Q)(eps_uc/hbar)[2n+1+sqrt((2n+1)^2+8 eta^2)]/eta^2 = 2 eps_uc/(hbar Q xi_opt), kappa_g^2 = M^2/(L_sq L_tot). Unconstrained: values > 1 are not attainable (see M_scan_H()).

docs.title: M_scan_H
docs.text:
M_scan_H(f_Hz, Q: float, L_tot_H: float, T_K: float)

M = sqrt(kappa_g^2 L_sq L_tot) at the scan-optimal coupling [H].

This is an unconstrained optimum; kappa_g^2 = kappa^2 L_in/L_tot <= 1 is required, so this raises where the optimum asks for more (e.g. low Q at low frequency). With a known input coil the tighter bound is kappa^2 L_in/L_tot.

docs.title: sweep
docs.text:
sweep(
    build: Callable[[Any], Any],
    values: Sequence[Any],
    *,
    workdir: str | Path = "runs/cavity_sweep",
    probes=None,
    probe_n: int | Sequence[int] | None = None,
    families: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    solve_kw: dict | None = None,
    refine: int = 0,
    min_step: float | None = None,
    refine_crossings: bool = True,
    track_kw: dict | None = None,
    verbose: int = 0,
    map_fn: Callable | None = None,
) -> Tracking

Solve build(v) (a Design) for each value, collect the modes and their probe vectors, and track() them; returns the Tracking.

Probes: 2D/xsec: probes = (p0, p1) flat arrays, default a probe_n grid (40 x 40) over the union of the cavity's bounding boxes at the first and last values (two extra solves; stored in <workdir>/probes.json and reused); 3D: probes = a list of [x, y, z], default probe_points_3d() of the first design (probe_n = (nx, ny, nz)), written into every design's fullwave.field_probes. solve_kw: passed to Design.solve (e.g. mpi_ranks). Each step is cached in <workdir>/step_<hash of the design document>/ (track_step.npz/.json): a re-run reuses it. refine: rounds of bisection of Tracking.needs_refinement() intervals (numeric values; not below min_step; refine_crossings: also crossings, to tell true crossings from narrow avoided ones). map_fn: optional parallel map over the values of one round, e.g. concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(n).map (the step function is a closure, so process pools cannot pickle it; 3D solves run as MPI subprocesses, so threads suffice).

docs.title: track
docs.text:
track(
    steps: Sequence[ModeStep],
    *,
    accept: float = 0.5,
    good: float = 0.9,
    degenerate_rtol: float = 1e-06,
    freq_weight: float = 0.1,
    gap_factor: float = 3.0,
    reject_floor: float = 0.2,
    doublet: float = 100.0,
) -> Tracking

Link the modes of consecutive ModeStep s into adiabatic branches and classify the crossings (module docstring). Steps are sorted by value (numeric, incl. numpy scalars) or kept in order.

accept: minimum overlap of a link (below it the branch ends and a new one starts); good: links below it, a competing second overlap (above half the best and above 0.3), or a rejected best match with overlap above reject_floor mark the interval ambiguous; degenerate_rtol: relative splitting below which modes form a degenerate cluster (their frequency order is noise: no crossing is read from it); freq_weight: weight of the frequency-continuity term in the assignment cost; gap_factor: an avoided-crossing window extends from the gap minimum until the gap exceeds gap_factor x the minimum (or stops growing, or the common range ends: truncated); doublet: pairs split by less than doublet x degenerate_rtol on both sides of a frequency-order change or a gap minimum are treated as a near-degenerate doublet (no crossing, no avoided crossing, links flagged doublet_mixing instead of ambiguous).

diabatic(
    events: Sequence[dict] | None = None,

Character-following (diabatic) branches: copies of the adiabatic branches whose tails are permuted at each avoided crossing (events: default all of kind "avoided"). A two-branch event swaps the two tails beyond x0; a multi-branch event applies its pair-minimum swaps in x order when they compose to its permutation (so the character is right between the minima too), else the permutation at x0. Within a few kappa/slope of a crossing every eigenmode is a mixture, so the diabatic quantities there are those of mixed modes.

docs.title: Receiver dataclass
docs.text:
Receiver(
    T_cav_K: float = 0.0,
    N_A: float | None = None,
    T_A_K: float | None = None,
    T_sys_K: float | None = None,
    T_in_K: float | None = None,
    n_cav: float | None = None,
    squeeze_dB: float = 0.0,
    squeeze_eff: float = 1.0,
    eta_out: float = 1.0,
    phase_sensitive: bool = False,
    eta_snr: float = 1.0,
    label: str = "",
)

Noise model of a single-port haloscope receiver.

Exactly one way of fixing the noise level:

  • T_sys_K: a total system noise temperature as quoted by the experiment, referred to the cavity port (flat in detuning; k_B T_sys per Hz). Overrides the physical noise model; only eta_snr still applies (eta_out must stay 1).

  • otherwise the physical model, in quanta per Hz referred to the amplifier input:

    N_sys(delta) = k [ eta_out N_port(delta) + (1 - eta_out)(n_in + 1/2) + N_A ], N_port = |chi|^2 S_cav (n_in + 1/2) + (1 - |chi|^2)(n_c + 1/2),

|chi|^2 = ((beta - 1)^2 + x^2)/((beta + 1)^2 + x^2) the cavity reflection, x = 2 Q0 delta/f, n_c the cavity-bath occupation (n_cav if given, else n_th(T_cav_K)), n_in = n_th(T_in_K) the occupation of the termination incident on the port AND of the transmission-loss baths (all at the fridge temperature; T_in_K defaults to T_cav_K), S_cav the squeezing delivered to the cavity (1 without squeezing), k = 2 for a phase-sensitive readout, else 1. This is 2301.09721 Eq. A4 (with alpha = eta_out, rho = squeeze_eff, G_S = 1/G_s). With an isolator at the cavity temperature and no squeezing, N_sys = k(n_c + 1/2 + N_A) is flat and independent of beta. T_in_K = 0 mimics "no isolator, cold amplifier input" (Kim et al. 2020 Sec. 3).

eta_out (HAYSTAC's alpha, 2301.09721 Table II): power transmission between the cavity port and the amplifier. It attenuates the axion signal (scan_rate and the limits multiply P by it) and replaces a fraction 1 - eta_out of the cavity output by fresh noise at n_in. N_A is then the added noise referred to the AMPLIFIER input (HAYSTAC's N_a).

N_A (quanta, excludes the input 1/2: SQL = 0.5) or T_A_K (classical HEMT noise temperature, N_A = k T_A/hf).

phase_sensitive=True (HAYSTAC phase II squeezed-state receiver, SSR): one quadrature is measured; the axion's random-phase signal puts half its power there, so the noise is reported in phase-insensitive-equivalent quanta N_sys = 2 N_quad, with N_quad counted so that vacuum is 1/2 (the convention of the corrected HAYSTAC analysis, arXiv:2301.09721 Sec. III, Eqs. A1, A3-A6). An ideal phase-sensitive amplifier without squeezing therefore gives N_sys = 1, the same as the SQL phase-insensitive one (no free lunch). N_A is then the single-quadrature added noise (HAYSTAC's N_a).

Squeezing convention (Malnou et al. 2019, arXiv:1809.06470): squeeze_dB is the squeezer's own one-quadrature gain G_s = 10^(dB/10) (noise reduction at the squeezer OUTPUT, before any loss). squeeze_eff is the squeezer -> cavity transmission eta_1 (HAYSTAC's rho = (alpha rho)/alpha), so S_cav = eta_1/G_s + 1 - eta_1 (2301.09721 Eq. 6 at the cavity). A squeezing MEASURED at the receiver output already contains N_A and eta_out; never enter it as squeeze_dB -- convert it with squeezer_gain_dB(), which removes N_A (otherwise the added noise is counted twice). The squeezer and the measured quadrature are centred on the cavity frequency, so chi(delta) multiplies both sideband quadratures by the same factor (chi(-delta)* = chi(delta)): no rotation of the ellipse, anti-squeezing never enters. This agrees with Malnou et al. Eq. 2. eta_snr multiplies the SNR (analysis efficiency, < 1), so the rate goes as eta_snr^2.

docs.title: scan_rate
docs.text:
scan_rate(
    f_Hz: float,
    cav: Cavity,
    rx: Receiver,
    *,
    g_GeV: float | None = None,
    snr: float = 5.0,
    Q_a: float | None = None,
    rho_GeV_cm3: float = 0.45,
    model: str = "DFSZ",
    prefactor: str = "optimal",
) -> float

Scan rate df/dt [Hz/s] reaching snr on an axion of coupling g.

Optimal weighting, dense steps: df/dt = eta_snr^2 int d delta [P(delta)/(h f N_sys(delta))]^2 / (SNR^2 Delta f_eff), Delta f_eff = f/Q_a, P = eta eta_out beta/(1+beta) Q_L P_coef L(delta). Q_a is the radiometer quality factor (f/Delta f_eff); None -> SHM, 6.78e5. Flat noise: (pi/4) (eta_c P_coef)^2 Q_L Q_a / (SNR k T_sys)^2, i.e. ~ g^4 B^4 V^2 C^2 Q_L/T^2. The separation of line shape and cavity response is exact in the dense-scan limit for any Q_L/Q_a, so there is no Q_L Q_a/(Q_L+Q_a) saturation here (cf. scan_rate_kim2020()).

prefactor="haystac": replace pi/4 by the 4/5 of 1611.07123 Eq. 5 (squared Lorentzians summed over steps of ~Delta nu_c/2, boxcar bins); use it with Q_a ~ 1e6. g_GeV None -> the benchmark model coupling (haloscope convention).

Axisymmetric design of the elliptical cell (elliptical_cell_contour) inside a conducting wall of thickness t (default 5 % of the equator radius): cavity region (mesh_size h, default Req/30) and wall surface mesh size wall_size (default h/3; the mesher also refines by curvature). With wall="polygon" the wall is the polyline (vertex spacing <= wall_size, denser near the iris by angle_tol, see elliptical_cell_contour()) and the mesh follows its vertices. target_f_Hz is scaled by 1/scale. wall_material as in axionmultiphysics.cavity.pillbox_design() (default lossless, G still reported). The design carries the contour in design.srf_contour (used by figures_of_merit()). wall: "smooth" (default) meshes the exact wall (elliptical arcs, contour shape) with curved second-order elements on it; "polygon" meshes the polyline (angle_tol), whose vertices are weak field singularities (docs/srf/README.md, "Wall representation").

tune_degeneracy(

    bracket=(0.8, 0.92),
    tol: float = 1e-05,
    design_kw: dict | None = None,
    workdir=None,
    verbose: bool = False,
) -> dict

Axial factor s (scaling the half-cell length and the axial semi-axes) at which the 2D pump and signal frequencies coincide: secant/Brent on Delta f(s) = f_signal - f_pump, each evaluation one axisymmetric solve. Every evaluation re-meshes, so Delta f(s) carries mesh noise at the level of the discretization error (a few kHz at h = Req/40, order 3, i.e. ~1e-5 in s): a tol below that only converges onto the noisy root. Returns {"axial_factor", "f_Hz", "history": [(s, f_pump, f_signal)], "design_kw"}.

    signal="TE011",

    subdiv: int = 4,
    with_fields: bool = False,

Heterodyne figures of merit of an axisymmetric cavity result (see the module docstring for definitions).

pump/signal: mode labels for find_mode(), or rows of res.cavity_modes(). contour: the cell contour (design.srf_contour; default res.design.srf_contour): mode labels, equator and A. Wall peaks: the solver's peak_wall_fields, the largest normal |E| and tangential |B| over the Gauss points of the wall faces evaluated in the cavity element (never at mesh vertices), the same field the 3D peaks estimate (figures_of_merit_3d()); face-rms variants and the tangential |E| (a PEC check) too. The peak ratios use the solver's B_rms, the equator values the lattice B0 (they agree to ~3e-5). Integrals: sub-triangle lattice of each element (subdiv) with the fields linear on each sub-triangle (converges as (h/subdiv)^2; the eigenvectors themselves converge with the mesh). Returns xi (pump, signal), f, the frequency splitting, eta_10, B_pk/B0 and E_pk/(c B0) of the pump (and of the signal, normalized by the signal's own rms B), A/V^(2/3), G (solver), V, and with with_fields the mode fields (cavity_mode_field dicts) under "fields".

docs.title: SRFGeometry dataclass
docs.text:
SRFGeometry(
    xi: float,
    eta: float,
    G_pump_ohm: float,
    G_signal_ohm: float,
    Bpk_over_B0: float,
    area_coeff: float,
    Epk_over_cB0: float | None = None,
    name: str = "",
    source: str = "",
)

Scale-free figures of merit of a cavity and its (pump, signal) mode pair.

xi: omega_0 = xi c V^(-1/3) (angular frequency; f_0 V^(1/3)/c is xi/2pi) eta: overlap eta_10 (C_01 = eta^2), NOT its square G_pump_ohm, G_signal_ohm: geometry factors in ohm, G = omega mu0 int|H|^2 dV / int|H_t|^2 dA, Q = G/R_s (the dimensionless natural-unit G times Z0 = 376.73 ohm) Bpk_over_B0: peak wall magnetic field of the pump / B_0 (B_0 = spatial RMS, peak in time), i.e. the largest |B| anywhere on the wall area_coeff: A_cav / V^(2/3) (>= 4.836, the sphere) Epk_over_cB0: peak wall electric field of the pump / (c B_0), dimensionless, informational: the pump's peak surface E is Epk_over_cB0 * c * B_0 (NOT times c B_pk).

The constructor validates every value (finite, in a physically possible range, and in the units above) and raises ValueError naming the field, so that a slipped convention (eta^2 for eta is the one it cannot catch; xi without 2 pi, G in natural units, B0/B_pk inverted, an impossible area) fails loudly instead of returning a plausible-looking design.

docs.text:
from_modes(
    modes: dict, *, bpk: str = "wall", **kw
) -> "SRFGeometry"

Build from the eigenmode side's figures of merit.

modes is either the output of axionmultiphysics.srf.figures_of_merit() (keys xi_pump, eta_10, G_pump_ohm, G_signal_ohm, Bpk_over_B0, B_equator_over_B0, A_over_V23, Epk_over_cB0) or a dict with this class's own field names. bpk picks the peak-field value:

  • "wall" (default): the largest pump |B| anywhere on the wall, 1.464 for the Project X cell shortened by 0.86 (iris-side lobe). This is the peak wall magnetic field, to which the field limit applies.
  • "equator": DIAGNOSTIC ONLY, the pump |B| at the equator (1.404). It is not the peak wall field: a design built on it runs the iris-side wall 4.3 % above the stated field limit. For an own-key dict it needs a B_equator_over_B0 entry.

docs.text:
scan_rate(
    f_a_Hz,
    f1_Hz,
    V_m3,
    B0_T,
    eta,
    Q_i,
    A,
    n_i,
    *,
    beta=None,
    tau: float = 1.0,
    n_e=0.0,
    target: Target = DEFAULT_TARGET,
    g_GeV=None,
)

Weak-signal dense-scan rate d(nu_1 - nu_0)/dt [Hz/s] (the angular-frequency rate divided by 2 pi):

d(omega_1 - omega_0)/dt = (pi^2/32) (Q_axion/Theta_95) g^4 rho^2 eta^4 B_0^4 V^2 Q_i
                          / (m_a omega_1^3) x G-bar_SRF(beta).

In SI with P0 = g^2 rho eta^2 B_0^2 V/omega_1 [W] (= 4 P_sig/Q_1) this is (pi^2/32)(Q_a/Theta) P0^2 Q_i G-bar/(hbar^2 omega_a omega_1). beta None -> beta_opt() at every mass. Vectorised over f_a (and any broadcastable argument).

docs.title: required_volume
docs.text:
required_volume(
    sc: ScenarioA,
    target: Target = DEFAULT_TARGET,
    *,
    omega1: str = "shifted",
    n: int = 256,
    adiabatic_eps: float | None = None,
    guard_Hz: float = 0.0,
) -> float

Smallest V [m^3] whose optimal scan covers the target band in the live time, with omega_0 = xi c V^(-1/3) and the coupling optimised at every mass. omega1: "shifted" (omega_1 = omega_0 + m_a, the definition) or "pump" (omega_1 = omega_0). adiabatic_eps: None (weak-signal optimum, no schedule constraint) or eps of tracking_rate() (e.g. 0.1).

guard_Hz: the resonance sweep is extended by this much beyond both band ends. The dense-scan rate assumes every target mass sees the whole detuning response and its whole (one-sided, upward) SHM line; without a guard the masses within ~ (Delta_c + nu_a v^2/2) of the ends are under-exposed (at 1 MHz an unguarded end collects only a few % of the statistic). The default, 0, integrates over the band only; 20 Hz guards raise V by 1.3e-4 here because the rate at the ends is fast.

docs.title: write_touchstone
docs.text:
write_touchstone(
    results: Mapping[str, Any],
    path: str | Path,
    kind: str = "S",
    z0: Any = DEFAULT_Z0,
    dense: bool = False,
    *,
    surface_losses: bool = False,
    passivity_tol: float = PASSIVITY_TOLERANCE,
) -> dict[str, Any]

Write the port parameters of a full-wave sweep as a Touchstone file (.sNp).

results: a results document (Results.data or results.json). kind: "S" (default), "Z" or "Y"; z0: reference resistance (ohm; one for every port, or for S one per port, written as a v1.1 option line); dense: the adaptive model's dense curve instead of the solved rows; surface_losses: add the resistive part of the perturbative conductor surface loss (port_parameters()). The values are in the engineering convention e^{+j omega t} (the engine's Z is conjugated), sorted by frequency, with a comment block giving the source, the port order and polarity, and the checks. Passivity violations (sigma_max(S) > 1 + passivity_tol) are warned about and written as computed. Returns the report of write_touchstone_data() plus source, Re_Z_unresolved_Hz and surface_loss_beyond_perturbation_Hz; its warnings holds every warning raised on the way.

docs.title: read_touchstone
docs.text:
read_touchstone(
    path: str | Path, nports: int | None = None
) -> dict[str, Any]

Read a Touchstone v1.0/v1.1 file (.sNp) with S-, Z- or Y-parameters.

nports defaults to the N of the extension. Handles the frequency units (Hz, kHz, MHz, GHz), the formats RI, MA and DB, the v1 defaults (# GHz S MA R 50), values spread over any number of lines, the 2-port order N11 N21 N12 N22, a v1.1 per-port R r1 ... rn (S-parameters only) and a 2-port file's trailing noise parameters (checked and ignored; noise_rows_ignored). Refuses data before the option line, Touchstone v2 keywords and H/G parameters.

Returns f_Hz, kind, z0_ohm (a float, or a list per port), data (n_f x n x n as stored but de-normalised: Z in ohm, Y in siemens), S and Z (both engineering convention, e^{+j omega t}), ports (names from an axionMultiPhysics port-order comment, else port_k), comments, option_line and noise_rows_ignored. S is always present (stored S, or converted where it exists); Z (and S of a Y file) is NaN at the frequencies where it does not exist (an open, an ideal thru, a singular Y), with a warning naming the file and the frequencies (Z_undefined_Hz, S_undefined_Hz).

docs.title: port_parameters
docs.text:
port_parameters(
    results: Mapping[str, Any],
    *,
    dense: bool = False,
    surface_losses: bool = False,
) -> dict

The port impedance matrix of a full-wave sweep, sorted by frequency, in the engineering convention.

results: a results document (Results.data or a loaded results.json) with fullwave.sweep. dense=False takes the solved rows (Z_matrix_re_ohm/Z_matrix_im_ohm, or Z_re_ohm/Z_im_ohm for a one-port 2D sweep); dense=True the adaptive sweep's dense model curve (fullwave.adaptive.dense, axionmultiphysics.circuit.fullwave_dense()). surface_losses=True adds the resistive part of the perturbative conductor surface loss of the solved rows, which Z does not contain (docs/physics/ fullwave_surface_losses.md): R_loss_ohm to a one-port's Re Z; for a multiport R_loss_matrix_ohm, which is the impedance perturbation only for in-phase port fields, so it is refused when that matrix has an imaginary part above 1e-6 of its norm or Z has a resistive part (radiation or bulk loss). The surface reactance (internal inductance, kinetic inductance) is not added. Rows where R_loss/|X| exceeds SURFACE_LOSS_PERTURBATION_LIMIT are warned about and listed (the perturbation is not accurate there).

Returns f_Hz, Z (n_f x n x n, ohm, e^{+j omega t}), ports (names in matrix order; port 1 is the pickup), port_details (polarity and terminals), source, notes (lines for a file header), Re_Z_unresolved_Hz (solved rows whose Re Z the solve's residual does not resolve; for dense=True the rows the model was fitted to), Re_Z_unresolved (per output frequency: flagged itself, or for the dense curve between flagged neighbouring solves), Z_relative_error (per output frequency, the estimated normwise relative error of Z: the rows' error indicator, signed where given, plus the solve's residual; the dense curve's model error; NaN when not known), Z_relative_error_source, Z_relative_error_kind ("normwise" for the rows; "proportional" for the dense curve, whose barycentric model shares one denominator over all entries, so that its error near a pole moves the entries together) and surface_loss_beyond_perturbation_Hz.

docs.title: z_to_s
docs.text:
z_to_s(
    Z: Any, z0: Any = DEFAULT_Z0, *, convention: str
) -> ndarray

Scattering matrix S = (z - 1)(z + 1)^-1, z = D^-1 Z D^-1, D = diag(sqrt(z0)).

Z: an n x n impedance matrix or a stack (... x n x n; a 1-D array is a one-port sweep) in ohm. z0: the real positive reference impedance, one value or one per port (ohm). convention: the time convention of Z ("axionmultiphysics" or "engineering", see to_engineering()). The result is in the engineering convention e^{+j omega t}, with the shape of Z (n_f x 1 x 1 for a 1-D input). Raises a ValueError naming the matrices where Z + z0 is singular (e.g. Z = -z0 for a one-port).

docs.text:
export_comsol(
    source,
    out: str | Path,
    *,
    format: str = "mphtxt",
    order: int = 1,
    workdir: str | Path | None = None,
    mesher: str = "",
    verbose: int = 0,
    class_name: str | None = None,
    feature_angle: float | None = None,
    physics: str = "none",
) -> dict

Export an axionMultiPhysics geometry or mesh to COMSOL.

source: a Design, a design dict, a design .json, an axmp-mesher .msh or a run directory (axmp solve -o DIR / axmp mesh -o DIR: holds mesh.msh or mesh3d.msh and design.json).

format: * "mphtxt" -- COMSOL mesh with named selections (designs are meshed first with axmp mesh into workdir, default <out>_mesh/); order=2 keeps second-order nodes. * "java" -- COMSOL Java API model that rebuilds the geometry (needs the compiled core for designs, or a run directory with mesh*_in.json). * "step" -- 3D designs: the OCC solids as STEP via axmp-mesher, plus <out>.solids.json.

physics: "none" (default: geometry and selections only) or "fullwave" (3D designs with a port pickup): the Java model, or for mphtxt the Import_<name>.java program, also gets the Electromagnetic Waves physics, materials, lumped ports, the axion source, a Frequency study and the Z/V exports (axionmultiphysics.comsol_physics). The design is needed: a design, a design .json or a run directory with design.json.

A model document (beta: a design with a top-level physics key, given directly, as a .json or as the design.json of a run directory) is refused with model.em_only_operation before anything is resolved, meshed or written: the export builds an electromagnetic COMSOL model.

Returns a summary dict (files written, entity counts, selections, approximations).

import_comsol(

Import path (a COMSOL .mph) and return an axionmultiphysics.Design.

out is the design JSON to write (default <model stem>_axmp/design.json next to the model's name in the current directory); the mesh, its info file and import_report.md/.json go next to it. route is "mesh", "replay" or "auto" (replay when the whole geometry sequence is supported, else mesh). Raises ImportError_ when something that changes the results cannot be mapped, unless allow_partial. The report is attached as design.import_report.

docs.title: decide
docs.text:
decide(
    E: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]],
    tol_eff: Mapping[str, float],
) -> dict

The refinement decision after the last level in E (E[family][level], levels 0..L): returns {"status": "accepted" | "not_converging" | "refine", "level": int | None, "family": str | None, "gain": float | None}.

Accepted when every family is within its tol_eff. Otherwise, from L >= 2, not converging when a family still above its tol_eff gained less than GUARD_TWO_HALVINGS over the last two halvings, E(L-2) / E(L) (the smallest such gain; ties to the alphabetically first family; E(L) = 0 is an infinite gain); otherwise refine. A family already within its tol_eff never stops the loop.
