docs.title: Mechanics and thermal¶
docs.text:
In lumped-element experiments, the static field pushes on the winding and everything bonded to it. Cooling from room temperature contracts parts by different amounts, while supports carry heat from warmer stages.

In this tutorial we compute these three effects on the quick-start toroid: \(R=H=2\,\mathrm{m}\), \(y=0.6\) and \(NI=10^6\,\mathrm{A\,turns}\).

We import axionMultiPhysics and set up plotting, run directories and a solve helper for the calculations.

docs.title: Magnetic forces¶
docs.text: We solve the toroid with force_samples=5000 to retain one force sample per winding mesh cell in res.forces["distributions"] for this mesh.

docs.title: Elastic deformation¶
docs.text:
We add a G10 ring pad in the \(1\,\mathrm{cm}\) gap between winding and sheath, a G10 ring post beneath the sheath with a \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\) wall and \(30\,\mathrm{cm}\) length, and a steel base plate under the post. Touching regions are bonded, with no sliding or separation. Every region whose material has a mechanical block belongs to the structure.

Nothing is clamped: both load cases below are self-balanced. The axionMultiPhysics solver removes the free axial translation and reports axial displacement relative to the assembly's volume-weighted mean, as the output warning states. Radial rigid motion does not exist in axisymmetry.

The material values are illustrative round numbers: Young's modulus \(E\), Poisson ratio \( u\), total contraction \(\alpha\) from room temperature, and conductivity \(k(T)\). G10 is orthotropic and is treated here as isotropic. G10 and steel are nonmagnetic, so adding them leaves \(L_p\) and \(\Psi\) unchanged; the output shows the same \(L_p\) before and after.

For axisymmetric, small-strain elasticity,

\[ abla\cdot oldsymbol\sigma+\mathbf f=0, \qquad oldsymbol\sigma=\lambda\,\mathrm{tr}( oldsymbol\varepsilon)\mathbf I +2\mu oldsymbol\varepsilon. \]

The strains follow from the radial and axial displacements:

\[ egin{aligned} \varepsilon_{rr}&=\partial_r u_r,& \varepsilon_{zz}&=\partial_z u_z,\ \varepsilon_{ heta heta}&= rac{u_r}{r},& \varepsilon_{rz}&= frac12(\partial_z u_r+\partial_r u_z). \end{aligned} \]

The Lamé constants are \(\lambda=E u/[(1+ u)(1-2 u)]\) and \(\mu=E/[2(1+ u)]\).

We define the support materials and geometry to solve for deformation under the magnetic load.

docs.title: Cooldown¶
docs.text:
cooldown adds each material's stress-free strain \(\varepsilon^{\mathrm{th}}=-\alpha\), where \(\alpha=\int_{T_{\mathrm{op}}}^{293\,\mathrm{K}}\alpha_{\mathrm{lin}}(T)\,dT\) is its positive integrated contraction \(\Delta L/L\) from room temperature to the operating temperature. Cooldown assumes every part ends at one uniform temperature. thermal_strain stores \(-\alpha\). The stress becomes

\[ \boldsymbol\sigma=\lambda\,\mathrm{tr}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon)\mathbf I +2\mu\boldsymbol\varepsilon+(3\lambda+2\mu)\alpha\mathbf I. \]

A free body of one material contracts without stress:

\[ \mathbf u=-\alpha\mathbf x,\qquad\boldsymbol\sigma=0. \]

Bonded parts cannot contract independently. Here \(\alpha\) is \(3.0\times10^{-3}\) for the winding, \(1.43\times10^{-3}\) for the niobium sheath, \(2.4\times10^{-3}\) for G10 and \(2.97\times10^{-3}\) for steel, so their mismatch creates stress.

The magnetic load remains included. Linear elasticity adds its displacement and stress to those from contraction.

We solve with cooldown to report the combined maxima and compare bonded and free radial contraction.

docs.title: Heat through the support¶
docs.text:
This solve is thermal only. Steady conduction obeys

\[ \nabla\cdot\bigl(k(T)\nabla T\bigr)=0. \]

The axionMultiPhysics solver interpolates the material's \(k(T)\) table piecewise linearly and uses Picard iteration. We hold only the sheath region at \(4.2\,\mathrm{K}\) and the base region at \(50\,\mathrm{K}\); all other surfaces are adiabatic. The post carries the whole temperature drop. The bonded pad and winding share the sheath temperature because they have no heat source and their other surfaces are adiabatic. heat_removed_W is the heat absorbed by the cold boundary: the load on the \(4.2\,\mathrm{K}\) stage.

For a uniform post of area \(A\) and length \(L\), the Kirchhoff transform is linear along the post:

\[ \theta(T)=\int_{T_c}^{T}k(T')\,dT', \qquad Q=\frac{A}{L}\int_{T_c}^{T_h}k(T)\,dT. \]

We solve steady conduction to compare the FEM heat load with this integral and with estimates using a constant conductivity.

docs.title: Quick start¶
docs.text: In lumped-element experiments, a static magnetic field lets axion dark matter drive oscillating flux through a pickup circuit. In this tutorial we build a toroidal axion detector, compute its signal coupling and pickup inductance, and inspect the fields. The installation guide covers setup; the cells below should be run in order.

docs.title: Geometry and field solve¶
docs.text:
templates lists the available designs. template creates a toroid with dimensions in metres; set changes a parameter. solve computes the static magnet and pickup fields and writes results under runs/nb_toroid.

The summary reports coupling, inductance, stored energy, and field peaks.

We import axionMultiPhysics and display its version and available designs to check the setup.

docs.title: Field inspection¶
docs.text:
show opens the viewer. quantities lists fields; quantity selects one and scale sets its color scale. pickup_Bmag is the magnetic field per ampere of pickup current. The last cell shows a meridional section through the toroid.

We open the viewer to inspect the computed fields.

docs.title: Results and exports¶
docs.text:
Psi is the signal coupling in H T m², L_p the pickup inductance in H, and F the scan figure of merit. \(\mathcal F/\mathcal F_{\rm req}\geq1\) meets the selected scan target (by default an illustrative one: DFSZ over 120.9 kHz–1 MHz in three years); the optimistic preset, an illustrative benchmark, assumes noise below the standard quantum limit. The benchmark also reports the stored energy and peak field the design needs to reach the requirement.

sample evaluates fields at cylindrical coordinates in metres. HTML and PNG exports save views. Mesh convergence should be checked before using numerical values for design decisions.

We report Psi, L_p, F, and the optimistic benchmark ratio, energy and peak field at the requirement.

docs.title: Full 3D¶
docs.text:
The commented example uses to_3d to revolve the geometry. Running it requires an MPI-enabled build, as described in installation.

We can uncomment the example below to solve the revolved geometry in 3D and view Bmag.

The schematic shows junctions, shunts, input coil and mutual inductance. Its helper requires running from examples/ in a source checkout.

We check the model formulas and display the first-stage schematic to show the circuit elements.

def curve(ch, f_lo, f_hi, n=300):
    # eta and eps_uc/hbar on a log grid; NaN at 50 MHz to break the line at the RT preamp switch
    f = np.geomspace(f_lo, f_hi, n)
    if f_lo < 50e6 < f_hi:
        f = np.concatenate([f[f < 50e6], [np.nan], f[f >= 50e6]])
    eta, eps = np.full(f.shape, np.nan), np.full(f.shape, np.nan)
    ok = np.isfinite(f)
    eta[ok], eps[ok] = ch.eta(f[ok]), ch.eps_uc_over_hbar(f[ok])
    return f, eta, eps

M_scan_H() raises for coupling beyond the global physical bound. The input coil should also be checked to ensure it can realize the returned mutual inductance.

We request coupling beyond the global bound to demonstrate the resulting error.

squid_for_resonator() supplies a SQUID model at the optimal mutual inductance, holding chain noise at the tuning frequency and converting to the circuit's spectral convention.

We assemble a tuned series readout and attach its SQUID to evaluate the optimally coupled circuit.

In [11]: Copied! 
f0, Q, T, L_in = 1e6, 1e6, 0.03, 2e-9
ro = ck.series_readout(L_p_H=LP, Psi_SI=PSI, f_Hz=f0, Q=Q, T_K=T, L_in_H=L_in, M_H=1e-9)
eq0 = ro.equivalent(f_Hz=f0)
w0, L_eff, QL, R0 = eq0["omega0_rad_s"], eq0["L_eff_H"], eq0["Q_loaded"], eq0["R_eff_ohm"]
print(f"f0 = {eq0['f0_Hz']:.6g} Hz, L_eff = {L_eff:.4e} H, Q_loaded = {QL:.4e}, R_eff = {R0:.3e} ohm")

chain_p = squid.chain("C1+low+RT", sign=+1)
ro.squid = chain_p.squid_for_resonator(f0, QL, L_eff, T)
sq = ro.squid

docs.title: dc SQUID readout chains¶
docs.text: In lumped-element experiments, a dc SQUID converts flux from a tuned axion pickup into an electrical output. Its measurement noise is correlated with circulating-current noise that feeds back into the pickup. An array and preamplifier add further noise. In this tutorial we follow the chain through resonator coupling and scan reach. The chain models (axionmultiphysics.squid) are beta.

docs.title: Noise parameters¶
docs.text:
For one-sided per-Hz power spectral densities,

\[ \eta(\omega)= \frac{\sqrt{S^{(1)}_{\Phi,\rm tot}S^{(1)}_J-(S^{(1)}_{\Phi J})^2}}{\hbar}, \qquad \epsilon_{\rm uc}(\omega)=\frac{S^{(1)}_{\Phi,\rm tot}}{2L_{\rm sq}}. \]

The spectra describe total flux noise, first-stage circulating-current noise, and their real cross-spectrum. \(L_{\rm sq}\) is the first-stage loop inductance; \(\omega\) is angular frequency. Dimensionless \(\eta\) accounts for correlation; \(\epsilon_{\rm uc}\) is uncoupled energy sensitivity in joule-seconds. Smaller \(\eta\) improves scan sensitivity at fixed detector and thermal noise.

We import the readout and scan tools and set plotting defaults for the calculations below.

docs.title: Presets¶
docs.text: C1 is the first stage alone. C1+low+RT adds a 48-by-3 SQUID array and room-temperature preamplifier. We tabulate \(\eta\), \(\epsilon_{\rm uc}/\hbar\), and noise with correlation removed to compare the presets.

docs.title: Custom devices¶
docs.text:
We set junction and loop parameters, then attach the later stages. validity() reports junction and thermal diagnostics; the Tesche–Clarke model assumes weak coupling and optimal bias. It omits \(1/f\) and quantum noise, later-stage backaction, and SQUID input loading.

We evaluate custom chains and a hot-shunt device to compare noise and check operating-regime warnings.

docs.title: Frequency dependence¶
docs.text:
Later stages increase imprecision at high frequency; RT preamplifiers switch at 50 MHz. Cryogenic curves begin at 5 MHz.

We plot both noise parameters against frequency to compare readout chains.

docs.title: Coupling to a resonator¶
docs.text: We specify the loaded quality factor, total inductance and noise temperature. M_scan_H() returns the mutual inductance in henries for maximum scan rate. We plot the coupling across frequency to compare this choice with noise matching at resonance.

docs.title: Detector and readout¶
docs.text:
Mesh convergence should be checked for each geometry.

We solve a toroid for pickup inductance and signal coupling, then rescale the signal coupling for the target magnetic field.

docs.title: Scan reach¶
docs.text:
We distribute three years uniformly in log frequency, adjusting coupling at each tuning. This assumes the required coupling can be realized throughout the band.

We compute and plot scan reach for the amplifier choices to compare their sensitivity.

docs.title: Correlation¶
docs.text: We compare noise spectra for sign=1, sign=-1 and zero correlation to assess how correlation affects sensitivity.

docs.title: Circuit drawings¶
docs.text:
axionmultiphysics[draw] is required to display the schematics.

We draw the SQUID chain to show its stages.

def solve(design, tag, **kw):
    """Solve in RUNS/tag and print the number of unknowns and any solver warning."""
    r = design.solve(RUNS / tag, verbose=0, **kw)
    # the cavity designs carry a nominal 1 T background field (for the form factor C, unused here): drop its warning
    w = [x for x in (r.data.get("warnings") or []) if "background field is present" not in x]
    dofs = r.data.get("mesh", {}).get("dofs")
    print(f"  {tag}: {dofs} DOFs" + (f", warnings: {w}" if w else ""))
    return r


def rel(a, b):
    return a / b - 1.0

    lab = srf.classify_modes(r, d.srf_contour)

def wall_profile(res, row, wall, n_per_seg=4, eps=1e-4 * REQ):
    """Arc length s, (r, z), |B_t| and |E| a distance eps inside the wall polyline (both normals tried; the one inside
    the cavity returns finite values). eps is large enough for every point to be located in the curved mesh."""
    W = np.asarray(wall, float)
    P, Tn, S, s0 = [], [], [], 0.0
    for p0, p1 in zip(W[:-1], W[1:]):
        L = float(np.hypot(*(p1 - p0)))
        if L == 0:
            continue
        for u in (np.arange(n_per_seg) + 0.5) / n_per_seg:
            P.append(p0 + u * (p1 - p0)); Tn.append((p1 - p0) / L); S.append(s0 + u * L)
        s0 += L
    P, Tn, S = np.array(P), np.array(Tn), np.array(S)
    N = np.column_stack([-Tn[:, 1], Tn[:, 0]])
    best = max((res.cavity_mode_sample(row, *(P + sg * eps * N).T) for sg in (1, -1)),
               key=lambda d: np.isfinite(d["H_phi"]).mean())
    Bt = MU0 * np.sqrt(best["H_phi"] ** 2 + (best["H_r"] * Tn[:, 0] + best["H_z"] * Tn[:, 1]) ** 2)
    E = np.sqrt(best["E_r"] ** 2 + best["E_phi"] ** 2 + best["E_z"] ** 2)
    return S, P, np.nan_to_num(Bt), np.nan_to_num(E)   # points on the axis (cap ends) may fall outside: 0

def budget(sc, V):
    """f0, U0, P_RF and A_cav of scenario sc at volume V (the formulas of design_A)."""
    g = sc.geometry
    f0 = float(g.f0_Hz(V))
    Q0 = g.G_pump_ohm / sc.Rs(f0)
    U0 = sc.B0_T ** 2 * V / (2 * het.MU0)
    P = 2 * math.pi * f0 * U0 / Q0
    A = float(g.area_m2(V))
    return dict(V=V, f0=f0, U0=U0, P_RF=P, A_cav=A)

docs.title: SRF heterodyne cavities¶
docs.text: In superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) heterodyne experiments, a cavity drives a pump mode whose oscillating magnetic field converts axions into a nearby signal mode. In this tutorial we tune their frequency difference to the axion frequency and calculate mode overlap, scan sensitivity and vibration limits. The SRF modules (axionmultiphysics.srf, axionmultiphysics.heterodyne) are beta.

docs.title: Mode overlap and size¶
docs.text:
The overlap amplitude and dimensionless pump frequency are

\[ \eta_{10}=\frac{\left|\int_V\widetilde{\mathbf E}_1^*\cdot\widetilde{\mathbf B}_0\,dV\right|} {\left(\int_V|\widetilde{\mathbf E}_1|^2\,dV\int_V|\widetilde{\mathbf B}_0|^2\,dV\right)^{1/2}}, \qquad \xi=\frac{\omega_0 V^{1/3}}{c}. \]

\(V\) includes beam-tube stubs, \(\omega_0\) is angular pump frequency, \(c\) is light speed, and tildes denote mode amplitudes. Both quantities are unchanged by uniform scaling.

We import axionMultiPhysics and set up solver helpers for the cavity calculations.

docs.title: Closed cylinders¶
docs.text: We compare axisymmetric solves with analytic results for three degenerate mode pairs.

docs.title: Elliptical cell¶
docs.text: We compare the original Project X contour with a shortened contour chosen to bring TM020 and TE011 together.

docs.title: Tuning the splitting¶
docs.text: We sweep the axial factor to locate the frequency crossing.

docs.title: Mode solve¶
docs.text: We solve the modes to inspect their labels, frequencies and residuals.

docs.title: Geometry factors¶
docs.text:
srf.figures_of_merit returns overlap, frequencies (Hz) and geometry factors (ohms).

We compute these quantities and field peaks to characterize the mode pair.

docs.title: Meridional fields¶
docs.text:
Opposite signs of the overlap density cancel in the volume integral.

We plot the mode fields and compare cell and cylinder overlap densities to show these cancellations.

docs.title: Equator fields¶
docs.text:
The green circle marks the pump field's sign reversal.

We plot the equator fields and overlap density to show their radial structure.

docs.title: Wall fields¶
docs.text: We plot the wall fields to locate their maxima.

docs.title: Comparison with 3D¶
docs.text: We revolve the contour into a cavity to compare 3D and axisymmetric results; this cell needs a build with the 3D engine and STRUMPACK (the 3D shift-invert eigensolver) and runs on four MPI ranks.

docs.title: Sensitivity¶
docs.text:
het.SRFGeometry.from_modes passes mode properties to the scan model. On resonance, for an axion line narrower than the signal linewidth,

\[ P_{\rm sig}=\frac14 g^2\eta^2 B_0^2\rho V\frac{Q_1}{\omega_1}. \]

This uses natural Heaviside–Lorentz units: \(g\) is axion–photon coupling, \(\rho\) axion density, \(\eta\) the overlap above, and \(Q_1\) the loaded signal quality factor at angular frequency \(\omega_1\). Python uses SI, with coupling in GeV\(^{-1}\) and density in GeV/cm\(^3\).

We compare geometry parameters from the solved modes with the preset to check the scan inputs.

docs.title: Required volume¶
docs.text:
het.design_A sizes a scenario (het.ScenarioA: surface resistance, peak wall field, flat receiver noise and wall temperature) for a band and live time (het.Target). The scenario and band below are round, illustrative numbers, not a proposed experiment: DFSZ over 0.2–2 MHz in one year. A is flat receiver noise in quanta; temperature sets wall noise.

We compare required volumes using the wall maximum and equator field.

docs.title: Signal statistics¶
docs.text: Weak-signal estimates require per-bin signal/background much smaller than one. We use het.required_volume_exact to compute volumes with the exact statistic, then recompute the RF load.

docs.title: Scan tracking¶
docs.text: het.scan_rate gives Hz/s; integrating inverse rate across the band gives scan time. We compare the scan rate with the resonance-tracking limit and recompute the required volumes with tracking imposed.

docs.title: Vibration requirement¶
docs.text:
Wall motion at the splitting frequency can scatter pump energy into the signal mode. The displacement amplitude spectral density must obey

\[ S_u^{1/2}\leq\frac{2\sqrt{2}\,L_c}{\eta_{\rm mix}} \left(\frac{\epsilon n_i\hbar}{U_0 Q_i}\right)^{1/2}. \]

Here \(\eta_{\rm mix}\) measures dimensionless mode mixing, \(L_c=V^{1/3}\), \(U_0=B_0^2V/(2\mu_0)\) and \(Q_i=G_{\rm signal}/R_s\); \(Q_i\) is intrinsic signal quality factor and \(R_s\) surface resistance. \(n_i\) is thermal occupation at the pump frequency and wall temperature; \(\epsilon\) is the tolerated noise fraction. The cell assumes unit mixing and a 0.1 noise fraction. Output is a bound in metres per square-root hertz, not a mechanical spectrum; smaller mixing relaxes it. Ideal axisymmetric TM/TE modes have zero first-order mixing; static asymmetry enables it.

We evaluate the bound for the illustrative scenario to quantify the vibration requirement.

docs.title: Chemistry (beta)
docs.text: Electrochemical cells and reactors are described by reaction kinetics and by the current that flows through the electrolyte between electrodes. In this guide we use axionmultiphysics.chem, which has two parts: 0D stiff chemical kinetics (a kinetics kernel, reactors, equilibrium and implicit time integrators, in axionmultiphysics.chem.kinetics) and the steady current distribution in an electrolyte (primary and secondary, 2D planar or axisymmetric, 3D on MPI ranks, and a 1D porous electrode). The module is beta: its interface may change, and its verification covers manufactured and closed-form solutions, stiff test problems and comparisons with Cantera and DOLFINx, but no published benchmark value or experiment.

docs.title: What is available
docs.text:
feature entry point build kinetics kernel: mass-action rates and their analytic Jacobians kinetics.mechanism, kinetics.rates every build reactors: batch, CSTR, semibatch, constant-pressure gas, adiabatic liquid, plug flow; equilibrium (index-1 DAE) kinetics.batch, cstr, semibatch, const_p_gas, adiabatic_liquid, pfr, equilibrium every build implicit integrators: BDF1..5, ESDIRK3(2), variable-order BDF, error control, dense output, events kinetics.adaptive, grid_bdf, grid_onestep, bdf_step, onestep_step every build current distribution, 2D planar or axisymmetric, P1/P2 chem.CurrentDistribution every build, one process current distribution, 3D tetrahedra, P1/P2 chem.CurrentDistribution3D MPI build, distributed 1D porous electrode (linearized Butler-Volmer only) chem.PorousElectrode every build mesh families (rectangle, annulus sector, graded disk; 3D box and sectors) chem.meshes, chem.meshes3d every build

Problems are set up in Python; there is no design-file, viewer or MCP interface. help(...) on each entry point documents the arguments.

docs.title: Kinetics and a parallel-plate cell
docs.text:
We integrate a first-order reaction in a batch reactor with the variable-order BDF method and compare it with its closed form, then solve the secondary current distribution of a parallel-plate cell with linearized Butler-Volmer kinetics, whose current density has a closed form (ohmic resistance plus two kinetic resistances):

import numpy as np
from axionmultiphysics.chem import CurrentDistribution, Reaction, meshes, FARADAY, GAS_CONSTANT
from axionmultiphysics.chem import kinetics as K

# 1. Stiff kinetics: A -> B with k = 0.7 1/s in a batch reactor, variable-order BDF with error control
mech = K.mechanism({"species": ["A", "B"],
                    "reactions": [{"reactants": {"A": 1}, "products": {"B": 1}, "A": 0.7}]})
tr = K.adaptive(K.batch(mech), "vsvo", 0.0, [2.0, 0.0], t_out=[1.0, 5.0], rtol=1e-8, atol=1e-10)
t, y = np.asarray(tr.t), np.asarray(tr.y)
print("steps:", tr.stats["steps"], " max |c_A - 2 exp(-0.7 t)|:", np.max(np.abs(y[:, 0] - 2 * np.exp(-0.7 * t))),
      " max |c_A + c_B - 2|:", np.max(np.abs(y.sum(axis=1) - 2)))

# 2. Secondary current distribution: a parallel-plate cell (gap L, height Hc) with linearized Butler-Volmer kinetics
L, Hc, kappa, i0, V = 0.01, 0.005, 1.0, 10.0, 0.05     # m, m, S/m, A/m^2, V
f = FARADAY / (GAS_CONSTANT * 298.15)
lin = Reaction("linear", i0)                            # i = i0 (alpha_a + alpha_c) f eta, alpha_a = alpha_c = 0.5
cd = CurrentDistribution(meshes.rect(16, 4, x1=L, y1=Hc), order=2)   # attributes: 1 x = 0, 2 x = L, 3-4 walls
cd.set_conductivity({1: kappa})
cd.add_electrode("anode", [1], reactions=[lin], phi_s=V)
cd.add_electrode("cathode", [2], reactions=[lin], phi_s=0.0)
rep = cd.solve()                                        # walls 3 and 4 are insulating by default
q = cd.boundary_quadrature([1], cd.boundary_degree)     # anode quadrature points: weights w, potential phi
i_num = np.sum(np.asarray(q["w"]) * i0 * f * (V - np.asarray(q["phi"]))) / Hc
i_exact = V / (L / kappa + 2 / (i0 * f))                # ohmic drop plus two kinetic resistances
print("Newton:", rep["converged"], rep["iterations"], " i =", i_num, "A/m^2  exact", i_exact,
      " rel. error", abs(i_num / i_exact - 1))

This prints (the last digits can differ between builds), after the one-time beta warning on standard error:

steps: 118  max |c_A - 2 exp(-0.7 t)|: 4.491919924909382e-08  max |c_A + c_B - 2|: 5.0182080713057076e-14
Newton: True 2  i = 3.3028336846435886 A/m^2  exact 3.302833684643331  rel. error 7.793765632868599e-14

The potential is linear across the cell, so the P2 solution reproduces the closed-form current to round-off; the kinetics error is set by the tolerances, and the sum of the concentrations is conserved to round-off.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• A mesh can also come from a model document: axmp.mesh(d).chem_mesh(order=2) returns a chem.TriMesh with the instance's boundary attributes and, on a curved mesh, its P2 edge nodes (a field of order 1 needs geometry order 1); see Meshes of model documents.
  • SI units throughout; anodic currents are positive; the overpotential is eta = phi_s - phi - E_eq. Axisymmetric meshes live in the meridian (r, z) and every integral carries r ("per radian"), while galvanostatic currents are 3D totals.
  • add_electrode(name, attributes, reactions=[...], phi_s=...) adds a kinetic electrode (potentiostatic, or galvanostatic with galvanostatic=True, current=I), primary=True, E_eq=... a primary one; boundaries without an electrode are insulating.
  • solve() raises chem.ConvergenceError when Newton does not converge; large cell voltages need continuation (initial="primary" in 2D, or solve_continuation).

CurrentDistribution3D needs the MPI build; the kinetics, the 2D current distribution and the porous electrode run in every build. Species transport, migration, double-layer charging, transient electrochemistry, impedance, battery models, temperature-dependent equilibrium constants and coupling to the fluids module are not implemented, and the porous electrode takes linearized Butler-Volmer kinetics only.

The walkthrough solves primary, secondary, 3D and porous-electrode problems against closed forms. The formulation notes give the details of the Python interface, the equations, the time integrators and the solvers, and the validation page lists the verification cases.

docs.title: COMSOL export and import
docs.text:
Lumped-element detectors and cavity haloscopes can be modeled in axionMultiPhysics and COMSOL Multiphysics. In this guide we use axionMultiPhysics to export a detector's geometry to COMSOL or read a saved COMSOL model into an axionMultiPhysics design. Exporting geometry lets us set up a calculation in COMSOL; importing a model transfers its mesh and supported electromagnetic settings. Neither conversion needs COMSOL installed on the conversion machine.

COMSOL and COMSOL Multiphysics are registered trademarks of COMSOL AB. axionMultiPhysics is not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by COMSOL AB.

docs.title: Design export to COMSOL
docs.text:
We export the toroid template design to Java so that its geometry can be rebuilt in COMSOL.

import axionmultiphysics as axmp
from axionmultiphysics.comsol import export_comsol

info = export_comsol(axmp.template("toroid"), "Toroid.java", format="java")
print(info["file"])

This writes Toroid.java, which rebuilds the geometry and named region selections. The returned dictionary lists the output file, selections and geometry approximations. On a machine with COMSOL, we run comsolcompile Toroid.java, then comsol batch -inputfile Toroid.class to create toroid.mph.

The default export contains geometry and selections; we assign materials and physics in COMSOL. To export the mesh instead, we use format="mphtxt" and an .mphtxt output path; a design is meshed first. A 3D design can also use format="step"; opening that file in COMSOL requires CAD import support.

For a 3D design with a gap-port pickup, physics="fullwave" adds supported materials, electromagnetic settings and a frequency study to the Java or mesh export. We check the returned summary for source and boundary approximations.

docs.title: COMSOL .mph model import
docs.text:
The import, and the 2D full-wave solver it uses for 2D models, are beta.

We save a 3D Electromagnetic Waves, Frequency Domain model with its tetrahedral mesh, using Mesh → Build All before saving. We then import the saved model and print its report summary to inspect the transferred settings.

import axionmultiphysics as axmp

d = axmp.import_comsol("detector.mph", "imported/design.json")
print(d.import_report.summary)

The returned Design uses the stored mesh. The output directory contains design.json, design.msh, design_mesh_info.json and an import report in Markdown and JSON. The printed summary describes the imported mesh and electromagnetic settings. We read the report before solving: it identifies transferred settings and approximations, including frequency-dependent materials represented by constant values. Unsupported physics that would change the result stops the import with an explanation.

2D and 2D-axisymmetric models import as well: they run on a 2D full-wave solver that takes the stored triangle mesh. Impedance, transition (thin layer) and scattering boundary conditions, and perfectly matched layers, are imported in 2D and 3D. The details and their validation are in comsol_import.md.

The API reference lists conversion options.

docs.title: Field maps for particle transport (beta)
docs.text:
A particle tracker needs the static magnetic field at arbitrary points, many millions of times, without the finite element solve. Results.export_field_map writes the field of a solved design as a field map: one regular grid (a patch) per region, each holding that region's own recovered field, refined until a fixed set of line integrals through the region agrees with the field to a stated tolerance. axionmultiphysics.fieldmap reads, evaluates and checks such maps. The format is axionmultiphysics.fieldmap/1.

Field maps are beta: their interface may change. The error control was calibrated on solved axisymmetric fields (a permeable sphere, superconducting and thin-layer sheets, iron cores, solenoids, a knee-law toroid) and checked on one 3D solve; the transport that reads the maps is not part of this version.

docs.title: Exporting a map
docs.text:
import axionmultiphysics as axmp

res = axmp.Design(doc).solve(workdir="runs/magnet")
fm = res.export_field_map("runs/magnet/fieldmap", tol=1e-4,
                          track_volumes=[{"name": "bore", "r": [0.0, 0.2], "z": [-0.5, 0.5]}])
print([(p.name, p.shape, p.record["accepted"]) for p in fm.patches])   # a patch not accepted also warns
B = fm.evaluate([[0.05, 0.0, 0.1]], patch="air+winding")   # Cartesian (x, y, z) in m -> (Bx, By, Bz) in T
option default meaning regions None the regions to map; None maps every region except ideal superconductors tol 1e-4 the RMS error of the map's chord integrals each patch must reach (0 < tol < 1) merge True adjacent regions with the same constitutive law and no curve between them share one patch track_volumes None boxes whose own chord families are reported: {"name", "r": [lo, hi], "z": [lo, hi]} (3D: "x", "y", "z") iterate_on_track_volumes False refine until the track volumes, too, meet the tolerance outside "refuse" what the evaluator does outside a patch's box: "refuse" or "zero" max_patch_MB, max_total_MB 512.0, 2048.0 caps on one patch's array and on all of them (MB = 2^20 bytes)

Axisymmetric results give kind 1 patches: (B_r, B_z, B_φ) on an (r, z) grid, interpolated bilinearly; Results3D gives kind 3 patches: (B_x, B_y, B_z) on a Cartesian grid, interpolated trilinearly. Planar and cross-section results are not mapped. A refusal writes nothing: neither path nor path.tmp exists afterwards.

docs.title: What a patch holds
docs.text:
One patch per region. Each region is served by its own grid, which covers the region's bounding box. Adjacent regions whose constitutive laws are equal (linear with μ_r equal within 1e-6 relative, such as air, windings and normal conductors, or the same nonlinear material) and whose shared faces carry no curve merge into one patch, named by its regions joined by + ("air+winding"). Ideal superconducting regions get no patch (B = 0 there) and are listed under zero_field_regions.

Curves. A superconducting sheet or a thin magnetic layer inside a region is an interface: the field jumps across it. A closed one splits the region into parts, each a patch of its own named <name>#k. An open one, which has the same part of the region on both of its sides, is refused with fieldmap.curve_in_region: no patch can hold a jump that ends inside it. Close the curve, or leave the region out. A sheet of a normal conductor (copper, say) is transparent to the static field: it is not an interface and is ignored (no split, no refusal, not listed in curves).

The recovered field B*. Within a patch the map represents B*, the finite element field B_h averaged at the nodes of a continuous space of the solution's order over the patch's own elements only, so averaging never crosses an interface with a jump. On the axis (kind 1, r = 0) B* has B_r = B_φ = 0, and B_z is the mean of the limits B_z = 2 ∂A_φ/∂r of the elements that have an edge on the axis.

Nodes. A grid node inside or on a patch element takes B* there (one-sided at the patch boundary). A node outside the patch whose grid cells reach the bounding box of a patch element takes the polynomial of the nearest patch element, continued to the node (never a neighbour's value), so that the stepper's trial points just outside the region see the region's own field continued. Other nodes hold 0. Kind-1 axis nodes hold B_r = B_φ = 0. The patch's box is the box of its elements' nodes, so a region whose faces lie on the box (a rectangular core) has no grid beyond them: points just outside are served by clamping (below).

How far the continuation can be trusted. Where a region's boundary lies inside the box (a curved interface, a sheet), the continued polynomial reaches about one cell of the final level past the boundary, and beyond that the grid holds zeros, which are interpolated without any refusal. In the sphere example (tolerance 1e-3) the air patch evaluated inside the ball, against the exact exterior field continued, differs from it by at most 0.8 % of B_patch at 0.25 final cell past the boundary and by up to 27 % at 1 cell (median 1.1 %); at 2 cells the error is large (median 14 %) and at 4 cells most points return 0. The depth shrinks as the map is refined, and the margin (below) does not extend it: the margin applies only where a region face is the box face. A stepper that visits points beyond a curved interface must keep them within a fraction of a final-level cell.

Field-free patches. A patch whose B_patch (below) is at most 1e-10 of the largest B_patch of the map, such as the inside of a closed superconducting sheet, is written as zeros (field_free: true) and not iterated on.

docs.title: Error control
docs.text:
Grids. Level 0 of a patch has n = max(9, ceil(L / h_el) + 1) nodes along each axis of its box (length L), with h_el the median element size of the patch (sqrt(2 × area) in 2D, (6 × volume)^(1/3) in 3D); each level halves the spacing (n → 2n − 1).

Chords. Each patch has fixed families of straight chords of nominal length 8 h_el, clipped to the patch (and, for kind 1, to r ≥ 0): bulk (16384, start points spread over all elements), layer (4096, start points within h_el of the patch's jump boundary: faces whose other side is another region or another part across a curve; not the outer boundary of the domain, not the axis), axis (4096, kind-1 patches that touch r = 0, start points with r < h_el) and track_<name> (4096 per track volume that meets the patch, clipped to the box). Kind-1 chords are lines in the (r, z) half-plane; kind-3 chords have isotropic directions. Start points are drawn element by element (probability ∝ area or volume) from a scrambled-Halton sequence whose seed is a constant of the format (chord_seed); the same chords serve every level.

The statistic. With B_patch the largest |B*| over the B* nodal values of the patch's elements, per chord c

e_c = |∫_c (B_map − B*) dl| / max( ∫_c |B*| dl , 0.1 L_c B_patch ),
n_c = |∫_c (B*  − B_h) dl| / the same denominator,

and, per family, E = RMS over chords of e_c (also its 95 % quantile and maximum) and H = RMS of n_c. The integrals of the map are exact (multilinear along a line); those of B*, |B*| and B_h use adaptive Gauss-Kronrod quadrature on the pieces between element boundaries. A chord is its intersection with the patch, found by walking it element by element (curved elements included): nothing of it is ever left out. An excursion shorter than the sampling step of the walk's point location (about 1e-5 m of closest approach to a curved interface) is not resolved: a chord that barely grazes the interface is counted as staying in the patch, which in the measured cases added up to a few mm (0.5-1 % of the chord) of the neighbouring region. A walk that cannot be completed (no element past a face, or more than a few tens of consecutive hand-overs without advancing along the chord) stops the export with fieldmap.chord_incomplete and writes nothing, rather than shortening the chord. Before any chord is drawn, a patch with an element whose Jacobian determinant is not of one sign at the nodes or the points between them (a tangled element) is refused with fieldmap.tangled_mesh. This is a second guard: the mesher repairs or refuses a 2D mesh with a tangled element, and the solve refuses one it reads (mesh.tangled, see "Curved elements in 2D" in the design format), so a solved design does not reach it.

Acceptance. A patch is accepted when E ≤ tol_eff = max(tol, 0.1 H) in every acceptance family (bulk, layer, axis; the track families too with iterate_on_track_volumes). The floor 0.1 H keeps the map from resolving the field ten times better than the solve represents it: when it acts, the family's record has floor_active: true and a note with both numbers ("the map tolerance was raised to a tenth of the FE indicator ...; a finer or higher-order solve lowers H"). H is an indicator of the solve's inter-element inconsistency, not evidence of its accuracy.

Guard and caps. From level 2 on, a family still above its tol_eff whose E fell by less than a factor 3.0 over the last two halvings stops the patch with the warning fieldmap.not_converging (written, not accepted). A patch whose next level would exceed max_patch_MB is written at the finest level that fits with fieldmap.cap_reached; a patch whose coarsest level does not fit is refused (fieldmap.patch_too_large), and so are patches that together exceed max_total_MB (fieldmap.total_cap_exceeded). A patch that is written but not accepted also raises a fieldmap.FieldMapWarning (a UserWarning) whose message starts with the code and names the patch, so that a script that does not read accepted still hears of it.

What the accuracy is for. A momentum scale inherits δ(∫B dl)/∫B dl. E is an RMS over a patch: along tracks confined to a small part of it the map error can be ten to twenty times larger, which is what track volumes measure. That the finite element field itself is accurate enough is a question for the solve (a finer mesh or a higher order), not for the map.

docs.title: Outside the maps
docs.text: FieldMap.evaluate(points, patch=name) interpolates the named patch's grid (a map with one patch needs no name). The evaluator never decides which region a point is in: the transport does, by the volume it is tracking in. Each patch record carries a margin (its level-0 spacing per axis; for write_map, the written spacing): a point outside the patch's box by at most the margin along every axis is clamped onto the box and gets exactly the value of the box's nearest point (a stepper's trial point just outside a volume whose faces lie on the box). A point farther out raises fieldmap.outside_map when the map was written with outside="refuse"; with outside="zero" it gets B = 0 and is counted in FieldMap.outside_calls. An export with outside="zero" records boundary_ratio, the largest |B*| on the outer boundary of the mapped domain relative to the largest B_patch, and warns with fieldmap.outside_field_not_small above 1e-3.

docs.title: The directory format
docs.text:
path/
  manifest.json
  patch_0/B.npy                       # shape (n_r, n_z, 3) or (n_x, n_y, n_z, 3), little-endian float64, C order, T
  patch_0/chords/<family>/start.npy   # and direction, segments, segment_chord, length, I_star, I_abs, I_h, I_map
  patch_1/...

Patches appear in the manifest sorted by name, in directories patch_<k> in that order; node i of axis a sits at origin[a] + i * spacing[a] (m). The manifest records the schema, units (m, T), tol, outside, the chord constants (chord_seed, chords), the control constants (control), the source (fe_solution: symmetry, design name and SHA-256 of the design document, SHA-256 of the static solution, order, elements, DOFs, version and build_info without the thread count, which timing records, and without the build's directory and file names), zero_field_regions, track_volumes, warnings, the patches and timing. Each patch record has its file and SHA-256, kind and frame (kind 3: a 4 × 4 placement transform, global = T local), regions, part (component) and bounding curves, box, h_el, grid (origin, spacing, shape), the history of E per level, B_patch, field_free, accepted, stop_reason (accepted, not_converging, cap or field_free), one record per chord family (n, E, E_q95, E_max, H, tol_eff, floor_active, gain_last, gain_two, acceptance), a pointwise report at 1e5 points (|B_map − B*| and |B* − B_h| relative to B_patch: 50 %, 99 %, maximum) and the normal-component mismatch with each neighbouring patch at the midpoints of their shared faces. The same results exported twice, with any number of threads, give identical arrays and manifests apart from timing; no string of a manifest outside timing is a local path.

fieldmap.write_map(path, patches, outside=...) writes the same format from nodal values given by the caller (an analytic field), with source: {"type": "nodal_values"}; fieldmap.load(path) reads either.

docs.title: Checking a map against its solve
docs.text:
• fieldmap.recovered_field(results, map, patch, points): B* of a patch at points in its native coordinates ((r, z) or (x, y, z)), NaN outside its elements.
  • fieldmap.chord_error(results, map, seed=None, patch=None): E and H of every family recomputed from the map read back from disk; with the manifest's seed it reproduces the report, with another seed it gives an independent estimate. Agreement within a factor 2.5 was measured on smooth cases (a sphere, sheets, a solenoid, a knee-law toroid); next to the singular corners of a saturated iron core E differed by up to 3.24 (the core) and 7.0 (the air beside it) between seeds, because a few millimetre chords at the corners hold most of E² there.
  • fieldmap.decide(E, tol_eff) is the refinement rule itself; fieldmap.halton(seed, n) and fieldmap.family_seed(seed, index) give the chord sequences.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text:
code when fieldmap.invalid_option a bad argument (tolerance, regions, caps, track volume, outside, a patch of write_map), an unknown or superconducting region in regions, a multi-patch evaluate without patch, planar or cross-section results fieldmap.curve_in_region a curve with the same part of its region on both sides (an open sheet) fieldmap.track_volume_empty a track volume that meets no mapped patch fieldmap.patch_too_large a patch whose coarsest grid exceeds max_patch_MB fieldmap.total_cap_exceeded the written patches together exceed max_total_MB fieldmap.outside_map evaluate at a point outside the patch's box by more than its margin, with outside="refuse" fieldmap.tangled_mesh a patch with tangled curved elements (Jacobian determinant changing sign, vanishing or inverted; a curved region much thinner than the mesh size at geometry order 2); refine the mesh or use geometry order 1; nothing is written. A second guard: a solve refuses such a mesh first (mesh.tangled) fieldmap.chord_incomplete a chord could not be walked through the mesh (an error of the builder: report it); nothing is written fieldmap.not_converging warning in the manifest: the two-halving guard stopped a patch fieldmap.cap_reached warning in the manifest: a patch was written at the largest level that fits its cap fieldmap.outside_field_not_small warning in the manifest: with outside="zero", the field on the mapped domain's boundary exceeds 1e-3 of the largest B_patch

Each error is an AxionMultiPhysicsError with code, a message naming the region, curve, patch or option, and a hint.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Bilinear and trilinear maps are not divergence-free; that matters only for tracking over very many turns.
  • The patch statistic is an RMS: a localized error is diluted by the patch's volume (track volumes report it).
  • The indicator H under-reports the finite element error (by up to about 14 in the measured cases).
  • Thin curved 3D shells waste most of their box and may reach the cap.
  • Next to singular corners (re-entrant iron, saturated cores) E is carried by a few chords and varies between chord seeds by factors of 3 to 7; it is reported, not gated.
  • Not in this version (described in the design): excluding the element around a re-entrant corner from the pointwise statistics, and copying the design's own convergence evidence (order 2 against order 3) into the manifest. The pointwise report includes the corner elements.
  • A placement (transform) is a rotation and a translation; write_map refuses a scale, shear or reflection.

docs.title: Fluids (beta)
docs.text: Viscous incompressible flow, heat carried by a flow and the Lorentz force on a conducting fluid in a magnetic field obey the Navier-Stokes equations and their couplings. In this guide we solve such problems with axionmultiphysics.fluids, an incompressible-flow library built on MFEM, and its builder axionmultiphysics.transport. Both are beta: their interfaces may change, and their verification covers manufactured, closed-form and cross-code problems but no published benchmark value or experiment. The module is compiled only in the MPI source build (installation); axionmultiphysics.build_info()["fluids"] says whether a build has it.

docs.title: Solvers
docs.text:
feature entry point geometry MPI ranks Stokes, Taylor-Hood P2/P1 fluids.solve_stokes planar; axisymmetric with swirl solve on any number; point evaluation on one 3D Stokes fluids.solve_stokes_3d tetrahedra or hexahedra, optionally curved distributed steady Navier-Stokes fluids.solve_navier_stokes planar; axisymmetric with swirl solve on any number; point evaluation on one inductionless MHD fluids.solve_navier_stokes(..., geometry="planar25d", mhd={...}) planar 2.5D (z-invariant) one transient Navier-Stokes (BDF1/BDF2) fluids.TransientNavierStokes planar; axisymmetric with swirl time steps on any number; point evaluation on one stabilized P1/P1 (GLS) fluids.gls_problem, fluids.solve_gls planar, enclosed flows one (serial) steady scalar (heat) transport, SUPG fluids.solve_heat, axionmultiphysics.transport.ScalarTransport planar; axisymmetric one steady Boussinesq natural convection fluids.solve_boussinesq planar; axisymmetric one

Problems are set up in Python from meshes, coefficients and boundary conditions; there is no design-file, viewer or MCP interface yet. The docstrings document the arguments (help(fluids.solve_navier_stokes)).

docs.title: Channel and cavity flow
docs.text:
We solve a Poiseuille channel with the steady Navier-Stokes solver, whose exact solution it reproduces to round-off, and the lid-driven cavity at Re = 100, steady and integrated in time from rest:

import numpy as np
from axionmultiphysics import fluids

# 1. Poiseuille flow in a channel [0, 4] x [0, 1]: steady Navier-Stokes at Re = rho U H / mu = 100.
#    Boundary attributes: 1 inflow (x = 0), 2 outflow (x = 4), 3 walls.
L, H, nx, ny = 4.0, 1.0, 32, 8
V = np.array([[x, y] for y in np.linspace(0, H, ny + 1) for x in np.linspace(0, L, nx + 1)])
vid = lambda i, j: j * (nx + 1) + i
tri = [t for j in range(ny) for i in range(nx)
       for t in ([vid(i, j), vid(i + 1, j), vid(i, j + 1)], [vid(i + 1, j), vid(i + 1, j + 1), vid(i, j + 1)])]
seg = [[vid(i, 0), vid(i + 1, 0)] for i in range(nx)] + [[vid(i + 1, ny), vid(i, ny)] for i in range(nx)] \
    + [[vid(0, j + 1), vid(0, j)] for j in range(ny)] + [[vid(nx, j), vid(nx, j + 1)] for j in range(ny)]
att = [3] * (2 * nx) + [1] * ny + [2] * ny
mesh = fluids.Mesh.from_arrays(V, np.array(tri, np.int32), np.array(seg, np.int32), np.array(att, np.int32))

rho, mu = 1.0, 0.01                                   # dynamic units: density, dynamic viscosity
profile = lambda x, y: (4 * y * (H - y) / H**2, 0.0)  # U = 1 on the centreline
sol = fluids.solve_navier_stokes(mesh, mu, rho, None, [
    {"attribute": 1, "kind": "dirichlet", "value": profile},
    {"attribute": 2, "kind": "do_nothing"},           # mu du/dn - p n = 0 (Laplacian form): p = 0 at the outlet
    {"attribute": 3, "kind": "dirichlet"}], form="laplacian")
d = sol.diagnostics
el = np.arange(mesh.n_elements, dtype=np.int32)       # evaluate at two reference points of every element
ref = np.array([[1 / 3, 1 / 3], [0.6, 0.2]])
x, _ = sol.geometry(el, ref)
u, _ = sol.velocity(el, ref)
p = sol.pressure(el, ref)
print("channel: converged", d["converged"], "| relative residual %.1e" % d["relative_residual"],
      "| max velocity error %.1e" % np.max(np.abs(u[..., 0] - 4 * x[..., 1] * (H - x[..., 1]) / H**2)),
      "| max pressure error %.1e" % np.max(np.abs(p - 8 * mu * (L - x[..., 0]) / H**2)))

# 2. Lid-driven cavity at Re = 100 on the unit square (attributes 1-4: bottom, right, top, left):
#    the steady solution, and the flow started from rest and integrated in time with error control.
cavity = fluids.Mesh.unit_square(16)
lid = lambda x, y: (1.0 if y > 1 - 1e-12 else 0.0, 0.0)
walls = [{"attribute": a, "kind": "dirichlet", "value": lid} for a in (1, 2, 3, 4)]
steady = fluids.solve_navier_stokes(cavity, mu, rho, None, walls)
print("cavity, steady: converged", steady.diagnostics["converged"], "after", steady.diagnostics["iterations"],
      "Newton steps")
ramp = lambda x, y, t: (min(t / 0.5, 1.0) * lid(x, y)[0], 0.0)   # time-dependent data take (x, y, t)
ts = fluids.TransientNavierStokes(cavity, mu, rho, None, [dict(w, value=ramp) for w in walls])
ts.initialize(lambda x, y: (0.0, 0.0))
run = ts.adapt(10.0, 1e-3, 1.0, 0.01)                 # to t = 10: rtol, velocity scale, first step
el = np.arange(cavity.n_elements, dtype=np.int32)
du = ts.snapshot().velocity(el, ref)[0] - steady.velocity(el, ref)[0]
print("cavity, transient: t =", ts.time(), "after", len(run["times"]) - 1, "steps (%d rejected)" % run["rejected"],
      "| max |u(t) - u_steady| %.1e" % np.max(np.abs(du)))

On one rank of an MPI build this prints (in a few seconds; the last digits can differ between builds), after the one-time beta warning on standard error:

channel: converged True | relative residual 1.5e-15 | max velocity error 1.1e-14 | max pressure error 3.8e-15
cavity, steady: converged True after 6 Newton steps
cavity, transient: t = 10.0 after 28 steps (1 rejected) | max |u(t) - u_steady| 4.8e-04

The parabolic profile lies in the P2 velocity space and the convective term vanishes on it, so the discrete solution is exact up to round-off; the cavity's transient solution approaches the steady one.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• A mesh can also come from a model document: axmp.mesh(d).instance(...).fluids_mesh() returns a fluids.Mesh that copies the instance mesh, with the boundary attributes of its named boundaries (im.attributes[name], im.remaining_attributes, im.axis_attributes); see Meshes of model documents.
  • Meshes are 2D in the (x, y) plane (fluids.Mesh.from_arrays, Mesh.unit_square, Mesh.annulus); axisymmetric problems use the meridional half plane (r, z) = (x, y), and fluids.Mesh3D.from_arrays builds 3D meshes.
  • Boundary conditions are a list of dicts, exactly one per boundary attribute; each solver's docstring lists the kinds it accepts.
  • solve_stokes and solve_stokes_3d are kinematic (everything divided by the density); Navier-Stokes, the time stepper, MHD and Boussinesq take dynamic units (mu, rho, physical pressure).
  • No solver raises on non-convergence: we check sol.diagnostics["converged"]. The fields of a solve that did not converge are refused.

  • A steady Navier-Stokes or MHD solve with strategy="newton" whose step stops reducing the residual at the round-off floor of its own residual evaluation (which can lie above newton_rtol on a fine mesh) stops there and counts as converged, provided the residual is still within a decade of newton_rtol. It says so: diagnostics["stopped_at_floor"] is then true and diagnostics["residual_floor"] holds the measured floor. So converged means diagnostics["relative_residual"] is at most newton_rtol, or at most ten times newton_rtol with stopped_at_floor set; a caller who needs the number itself reads it. The stop accepts the iterate it fired on, so the residual it reports can be a little larger than the one the full iteration budget would have wandered to (on the finest Ha = 0 level of analytic_hartmann_2d with STRUMPACK: 1.14e-12 at the stop, 9.97e-13 after 22 steps without it). The measured floor depends on the number of MPI ranks at round-off level, so a solve sitting at the floor may stop a step earlier or later, and report a slightly different residual, on another rank count; converged can then differ between a serial and a parallel run. residual_floor_factor=0 switches the rule off, and strategy="picard" and "ptc", the time steps, solve_gls and solve_boussinesq never use it. The formulation notes derive the floor and list its measured values.

  • A verdict rests on linear algebra, and the solvers report how accurate it was: diagnostics["lu_residual_max"] (the direct solves; each history entry has its own lu_residual) and diagnostics["mass_lu_residual_max"] (the mass solves behind the dual norm). A final direct solve above max(newton_rtol, 1e-11) or a mass solve above 1e-10 makes the solve report converged = false, with the reason in diagnostics["failure"].

  • TransientNavierStokes.initialize() returns False when the projection of the initial field onto the discretely divergence-free fields misses its accuracy gate (1e-13 on the backward error of the projection solve, at every newton_rtol, on any domain shape and in any length unit). We check that return value: after a False, advance, step_trial, adapt and snapshot raise an error naming the projection. ts.diagnostics["projection_residual"] and ts.diagnostics["projection_converged"] hold the residual and the verdict. STRUMPACK (the default direct solver of a build that has it) misses this gate on some scaled or stretched domains, depending on the processor; pass lu="eigen" there (the error says so).
  • quad_order_convection=0 (the default) integrates the convective term exactly for the element shape and geometric order of the mesh; a rule that under-integrates it is refused.

3D Stokes is the only distributed solver; the 2D solves can run on several ranks, but their fields are evaluated on one, and transport, Boussinesq, MHD and GLS run on one rank. Turbulence models, compressible flow, induced magnetic fields and 3D Navier-Stokes are not implemented.

The walkthrough solves Stokes problems step by step against exact solutions. The formulation notes give the details of the Python interface, the equations, the discretization (including the stabilized equal-order elements) and the solvers, and the validation page lists the verification cases.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: In axion dark-matter experiments, finite-element calculations describe detector fields. On this page we install axionMultiPhysics, which uses a C++17 core for these calculations and Python for building designs and inspecting results. The 3D engine requires MPI-enabled MFEM and hypre; sequential builds support axisymmetric calculations. Once the 0.2.0 wheels are on PyPI (see the note below), on Linux x86_64 and macOS a wheel is the quickest install; it has everything except the 3D engine and the fluids module, which need the MPI source build below.

docs.title: Wheel from PyPI
docs.text:
The 0.2.0 wheels follow on PyPI after the release; until pip index versions axionmultiphysics lists 0.2.0, pip install axionmultiphysics installs 0.1.0, whose API lacks the 0.2.0 features. Until then we install 0.2.0 from source (build and installation below). The commands in this section apply once the wheels are listed.

python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate     # Python 3.10 or newer
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install "axionmultiphysics[mesh,notebook]"

The mesh extra installs gmsh's own wheel, which axionMultiPhysics's mesher loads (why it is an extra). On Linux that wheel needs a few X11/OpenGL libraries even without a display (Debian/Ubuntu: sudo apt-get install libglu1-mesa libgl1 libxcursor1 libxft2 libxinerama1). Wheels are built for manylinux_2_28 x86_64 and for macOS 11+ on x86_64 and arm64, for CPython 3.10–3.14 (what a wheel contains). On other platforms, and for the 3D engine, we build from source.

docs.title: Build and installation
docs.text: The build requires Python 3.10+ with development headers, a C++17 compiler, CMake 3.20+, Ninja and curl, and for the MPI build also MPI and BLAS/LAPACK. We build and install axionMultiPhysics in a virtual environment so that the build tools and package use the same Python interpreter. These commands are tested in clean Ubuntu 24.04 and Rocky Linux 9 containers (docker/) and with a Cray programming environment, and the sequential build was tested on macOS (arm64) in CI before 0.2.0; 0.2.0 itself was built and tested on Linux x86_64 only, the MPI build has not been tested on macOS, and Windows is not supported.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Debian/Ubuntu

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install build-essential cmake ninja-build pkg-config git curl ca-certificates \
    python3-dev python3-venv libopenmpi-dev openmpi-bin libopenblas-dev liblapack-dev

On Ubuntu 24.04 we use OpenMPI: its MPICH package builds axionMultiPhysics, but its mpirun starts every rank as a separate one-rank job.

RHEL 9 and its rebuilds (Rocky, Alma)

sudo dnf install epel-release dnf-plugins-core && sudo dnf config-manager --set-enabled crb
sudo dnf install gcc gcc-c++ make cmake ninja-build pkgconf-pkg-config git tar gzip \
    python3.12 python3.12-devel openmpi-devel openblas-devel
export PATH=/usr/lib64/openmpi/bin:$PATH    # or: module load mpi/openmpi-x86_64

The system Python of RHEL 9 is 3.9, so the virtual environment below is created with python3.12.

macOS (Homebrew)

xcode-select --install
brew install cmake ninja open-mpi libomp python@3.12

Homebrew's Python is python3.12; BLAS/LAPACK come from Apple's Accelerate framework.

On a shared cluster, we load a C++17 compiler, MPI, CMake and Python with the site's modules and run compilation in a compute allocation. The compiler and MPI environment should remain available when using the installed package. On Cray systems the dependency scripts take MPICC=cc MPICXX=CC.

docs.title: MPI source build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/bsafdi/axionMultiPhysics && cd axionMultiPhysics
python3 -m venv .venv      # Python 3.10 or newer; on macOS (Homebrew) and RHEL 9: python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
pip install "scikit-build-core>=0.9" "nanobind>=2.0" numpy
bash scripts/fetch_deps.sh
bash scripts/build_deps.sh
cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
cmake --build build
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure
pip install --no-build-isolation -e ".[test]"

The dependency scripts download and build MFEM, hypre, METIS and the other pinned libraries. CMake builds libaxionmultiphysics, the Python bindings, axmp and the separate gmsh mesher. It detects MPI support from MFEM and then also builds the fluids module (beta). ctest checks the C++ components; the final command installs the Python package. For the example notebooks and the MCP server we install the extras instead: pip install --no-build-isolation -e ".[notebook,plots,draw,mcp,test]". With a threaded OpenBLAS (Ubuntu's default), we set export OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 before running; source scripts/env.sh sets it.

docs.title: Sequential source build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/bsafdi/axionMultiPhysics && cd axionMultiPhysics
python3 -m venv .venv      # Python 3.10 or newer; on macOS (Homebrew) and RHEL 9: python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install --upgrade pip
bash scripts/build_deps_wheel.sh
AXIONMULTIPHYSICS_DEPS=$PWD/third_party/install-seq pip install ".[all,test]"

This build needs no MPI or BLAS/LAPACK and is the configuration of the wheels. It has everything except the 3D engine, the fluids module and the 3D current distributions of the chemistry module. Its mesher uses gmsh's PyPI wheel, which on Linux needs a few X11/OpenGL libraries even without a display (Debian/Ubuntu: libglu1-mesa libgl1 libxcursor1 libxft2 libxinerama1).

Build options and packaging describes the wheels, every CMake option, the optional STRUMPACK and GPU builds, clusters and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Python installation check
docs.text:
We inspect the build information to check the available engines.

import axionmultiphysics as axmp

print(axmp.build_info())

The dictionary reports versions, device, threads and available engines. For the MPI source build, mpi and engine_3d should both be True. A false engine_3d means an MPI-enabled build is needed for 3D designs. The next step is the quick start; JupyterLab is installed separately if needed with pip install jupyterlab.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Installation puts axmp on PATH. These commands cover a typical design-to-results workflow:

Command Result axmp template toroid > design.json Writes a starting design. axmp validate design.json Checks the design's structure and values. axmp mesh design.json -o run Generates a mesh in run/. axmp solve design.json -o run --scene Writes run/results.json and run/scene.json. axmp render run/scene.json -o field.png Renders a field image. axmp schema Prints the design JSON Schema.

Running axmp without arguments displays usage. mpirun -n N axmp solve design.json -o run solves a 3D design on N MPI ranks. The corresponding workflows are described in Designs and solvers, Visualization and COMSOL export and import.

docs.title: Chat assistants (MCP)
docs.text: Lumped-element detectors, cavity haloscopes and SRF heterodyne detectors search for axion dark matter. In this guide we configure chat assistants to use axionMultiPhysics's server for the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard through which chat assistants such as Claude Code and Claude Desktop call external tools. With it, an assistant can build, solve, plot and optimize lumped-element detector designs and work with the beta modules for cavity haloscopes, SRF heterodyne detectors and dc SQUID readout chains and with COMSOL files on the local machine through axionMultiPhysics; the results it reports are the solver's.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
In the source checkout from the Installation page, install the MCP extra (after the MPI build; after the sequential build, AXIONMULTIPHYSICS_DEPS=$PWD/third_party/install-seq pip install ".[mesh,mcp]"):

pip install --no-build-isolation -e ".[mcp]"

Once the 0.2.0 wheels are on PyPI, the same extra is pip install "axionmultiphysics[mcp]". The server is the command axionmultiphysics-mcp in the environment's bin directory.

The server keeps designs (designs/<name>.json) and results (runs/<name>/) in the directory AXMP_WORKSPACE (default ./axmp_workspace). It inherits the environment of the client that starts it, so we set AXMP_WORKSPACE (and, if needed, AXMP_THREADS, AXMP_MESHER or LD_LIBRARY_PATH) in the client configuration.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
We register the server with Claude Code to enable axionMultiPhysics tool calls.

claude mcp add axionmultiphysics -e AXMP_WORKSPACE=$HOME/axmp_workspace -- /path/to/axionMultiPhysics/.venv/bin/axionmultiphysics-mcp

docs.title: Claude Desktop
docs.text:
We add the server to claude_desktop_config.json to enable axionMultiPhysics tool calls.

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "axionmultiphysics": {
      "command": "/path/to/axionMultiPhysics/.venv/bin/axionmultiphysics-mcp",
      "env": {"AXMP_WORKSPACE": "/path/to/axmp_workspace"}
    }
  }
}

Other MCP clients that start a local (stdio) server take the same command and environment. Some clients stop waiting for a tool after a fixed time; for long sweeps and optimizations, we raise the client's tool timeout if it has one.

The assistant should start with the axionmultiphysics_guide tool, which explains the workflow, units and conventions; most clients read it automatically when the server starts.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
User: “Build an ABRACADABRA-style toroid with R = H = 2 m and inner radius ratio y = 0.6, solve it, show me a section plot and tell me the pickup inductance and the signal coupling.”

The assistant calls create_design (template "toroid", R = 2, H = 2, y = 0.6), solve_design and render_design (section, Bmag).

Assistant: “The pickup inductance is L_p ≈ 1.458 µH and the signal coupling is Ψ ≈ 3.09 × 10⁻⁷ H T m² (0.246 T m³ in natural units). The static field stays inside the winding box and falls off as 1/r, from 0.167 T at the inner wall to 0.10 T at the outer wall, matching μ₀NI/(2π · 1.2 m). L_p computed from flux and from energy agrees to 5 × 10⁻¹³. To reach the optimistic benchmark the peak field would have to rise to about 7.4 T.”

A convergence check (order 3) should be requested and the warnings read before quoting a number.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text: Tool Purpose axionmultiphysics_guide Workflow, units and physics conventions list_templates, create_design, put_design, get_design, list_designs, design_schema Starting from a template or writing a design document set_parameters Changing parameters of a saved design, or saving a variant under a new name solve_design Meshing and solving: Ψ, L_p, F, fields, forces, benchmarks, cost metric render_design, start_viewer PNG section or 3D cutaway; live browser viewer requirement F_req for a noise benchmark sweep Solving for several values of one parameter sensitivities, list_objectives Shape derivatives of the figures of merit optimize_design, optimize_global, optimize Gradient-based (adjoint), global (differential evolution) or derivative-free (bounded Powell) optimization set_fullwave, set_hts, make_3d, list_conductors Full-wave sweep, HTS screening currents, 3D designs, conductor critical surfaces list_jobs, cancel_job Following or stopping long jobs

docs.title: Other detector types
docs.text:
These tools wrap the same Python functions as the walkthroughs for cavity haloscopes, SRF heterodyne detectors, dc SQUID readout chains and COMSOL export and import. The cavity, SRF and SQUID modules, and the COMSOL importer, are beta.

Tool Purpose cavity_presets, cavity_preset_limit Published cavity haloscope runs and the exclusion recomputed from their numbers cavity_scan Scan rate, optimal coupling, excluded coupling and time to cover a band for one cavity mode create_cavity Pillbox or coaxial cavity design; solve_design then returns its modes, form factors and Q srf_design, srf_mode_pair Volume, frequency, RF power and cost metric of an SRF heterodyne detector (geometry: projectx, the computed default cell, or equator_diagnostic); figures of merit of a mode pair squid_chain, squid_reach Added noise of a dc SQUID readout chain; reach of a solved design read out by it export_comsol, inspect_comsol, import_comsol Writing a design for COMSOL; summarising or importing a .mph file export_touchstone A solved design's full-wave S-, Z- or Y-parameters as a Touchstone v1 file, with passivity and reciprocity checks

Asked for the scan rate of a cavity at 5.75 GHz with B = 9 T, V = 1.5 L, C = 0.5, Q0 = 30 000, a quantum-limited amplifier and the cavity at 50 mK, the assistant called cavity_scan and reported 4.6 Hz/s at the KSVZ coupling, with β = 2, and 125 days to cover 5.75–5.80 GHz.

docs.title: Meshes of model documents (beta)
docs.text:
A planar or axisymmetric model document with regions can be meshed in this version, and its named boundaries can be listed and checked. Nothing solves it yet: this is the geometry half of the model path. 3D model documents and model documents on an imported mesh (mesh.file) are refused with route.not_implemented.

The mesher is the separate program axmp-mesher (it runs gmsh). Where it does not run (a wheel installed without the mesh extra, or without the X11/OpenGL libraries gmsh needs), axmp validate lists the unavailable finding build.requires_mesher first, with the install hint, and the commands below refuse the document with it. A document without a geometry (a reactor) or on an imported mesh needs no mesher.

docs.title: A split rectangle
docs.text:
{
  "schema": "axionmultiphysics.design/1", "name": "split_rect", "symmetry": "planar",
  "parameters": {"L": 0.04, "H": 0.01},
  "materials": {"slab": {"density": 998, "thermal": {"k_W_mK": 0.6, "cp_J_kgK": 4180}}},
  "regions": [
    {"name": "a", "shape": {"rect": {"x": [0, "L/2"], "y": [0, "H"]}}, "material": "slab"},
    {"name": "b", "shape": {"rect": {"x": ["L/2", "L"], "y": [0, "H"]}}, "material": "slab"}],
  "curves": [{"name": "mk_line", "path": {"segment": [["L/4", 0], ["L/4", "H"]]}}],
  "boundaries": {"hot": {"of": "a", "where": {"x": 0}}, "cold": {"of": "b", "where": {"x": "L"}},
                 "interface": {"between": ["a", "b"]}, "mk": {"curve": "mk_line"}},
  "physics": {"heat": {"type": "heat.transfer", "domains": ["a", "b"],
    "boundary_conditions": {"hot": {"kind": "temperature", "T_K": 310}, "cold": {"kind": "temperature", "T_K": 290},
                            "remaining": {"kind": "insulation"}}}},
  "outputs": {"Q_mk": {"kind": "flux", "of": "heat", "on": "mk"}},
  "mesh": {"size": "H/8"}
}

docs.title: axmp boundaries
docs.text:
axmp boundaries split_rect.json            # a text table
axmp boundaries split_rect.json --json     # the same as JSON
axmp boundaries split_rect.json --json --mesh -o run   # also mesh into run/ and count the faces

It validates the document (with the mesher probe), runs the mesher's resolve pass, then the full check: the checks that axmp validate can only defer because they need the geometry. They are the empty selections (boundary.empty_selection), the partition rule of every physics (physics.boundary_uncovered, physics.boundary_double, physics.boundary_interior, physics.boundary_outside_domain), the partial matches (boundary.partial_match, a warning), and the outputs on resolved boundaries (output.boundary_not_in_domain, output.force_on_interior, output.force_needs_stress_form). After it the report's deferred list is empty.

The JSON is the validation report with three keys added:

  • symmetry;
  • boundaries: one row per boundary name with selector (as written), entities, measure and measure_units ("m", the length), area_m2 (the revolved area, axisymmetric only), bbox (exact, keyed by the coordinate names), point, adjacent (the region pairs, exterior last) and used_by: the conditions keyed by the boundary (physics, kind, and the part the physics takes: a key is taken where its boundary lies on the domain boundary of that physics) then the outputs on it;
  • edges: every boundary edge, sorted by its point, with adjacent, type, bbox, point, measure, names (the boundaries that select it; empty for an edge no boundary names, which "remaining" covers) and axis.

With --mesh every row and edge also has faces, its number of boundary elements on the mesh (with the document's mesh.refinements). No master number or geometry-kernel tag appears anywhere.

With an error the command prints the report with ok false and the first error's fields at the top level, the table included when the boundaries could be resolved (the hints send you to it), and exits with status 1.

docs.title: axmp mesh
docs.text:
axmp mesh split_rect.json -o run

removes the mesh.msh, mesh_info.json and mesh_in.json of an earlier run in run/ before it does anything else, so no refusal leaves an earlier mesh behind, then runs the same checks before it meshes. When one fails, no mesh is written; if the check that failed needs the geometry, the mesher's resolve pass has left its mesh_in.json (with "resolve_only": true), mesh_info.json and mesh_mesher.log in run/. When all pass it writes run/mesh_in.json (the mesher's input), run/mesh.msh, run/mesh_info.json (which lists the atoms and their master numbers) and run/mesh_mesher.log. It prints ok, name, symmetry, geometry_order, the three paths, boundaries (measure, measure_units and, for an axisymmetric model, area_m2) and the warnings. A failed mesher run is mesh.generation_failed, with the mesher's error in the message and the log's path in the hint. The geometry order is mesh.geometry_order, else the largest order every physics takes (mesh.geometry_order_lowered warns when that is 1 for a curved model). axmp validate takes --mesher too, for its probe.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
import axionmultiphysics as axmp

d = axmp.load("split_rect.json")
table = d.boundaries()                 # the --json report; raises the first error
m = axmp.mesh(d, workdir="run")        # MeshedModel; without workdir a temporary directory is used and removed
m.symmetry, m.geometry_order, m.regions   # regions: {"a": {"area_m2": ...}, ...} ("volume_m3" too when axisymmetric)
m.boundaries                           # the table's rows, without face counts
im = m.instance("a")                   # a region or domain name, a list of names, or None for every region
im.attributes["hot"]                   # instance boundary attributes of a boundary: list[int], 1..n
im.remaining_attributes, im.axis_attributes
im.vertices(), im.elements(), im.boundary(), im.boundary_attributes(), im.element_attributes()
fp = im.face_points("mk", order=4)     # points, weights and normals for a flux integral

face_points(name=None, *, order, attribute=None) takes exactly one of a boundary (or section) name and an instance attribute, which is the way to the edges no boundary names and to the axis. It returns NumPy arrays faces (m,), elements (m,), ref (m, q, 2), weights (m, q) (the face Jacobian is included, so they sum to the length), normals (m, q, 2) and points (m, q, 2). The normals are outward on the boundary of the instance; on a section (a boundary interior to the instance) they have the orientation of the selection: from A to B for between, outward from D for of, the written direction of a curve marker turned by +90 degrees. section(name) gives the faces of an interior boundary with their signs and length. The instance mesh owns its data: it works after the MeshedModel is gone. Misuse (an unknown name, a boundary with no face on the instance, an attribute that is not on it, both or neither argument) is a ValueError; an electromagnetic design given to Design.boundaries() or axmp.mesh is refused with a message and no code.

axmp.mesh meshes into its working directory every time and reads what that run wrote.

docs.title: Handing a mesh to the engines
docs.text:
im.fluids_mesh() and im.chem_mesh(order=2) give an instance mesh to the fluids and chemistry engines (m.fluids_mesh(domain=None) and m.chem_mesh(domain=None, order=2) are shorthands for m.instance(domain) followed by the call). The engines take no document yet (nothing solves a model document in this version), so the conditions are yours to write, on the instance's own attribute numbers: im.attributes[name], im.remaining_attributes and im.axis_attributes. A master number is not a boundary attribute of the instance mesh, and both engine families refuse one.

import numpy as np
import axionmultiphysics as axmp
from axionmultiphysics import fluids

# Plane Poiseuille flow through a channel of height H (a model document with a geometry and its named boundaries)
L, H, U, nu = 0.04, 0.01, 0.01, 1e-6
d = {"schema": "axionmultiphysics.design/1", "name": "channel", "symmetry": "planar",
     "parameters": {"L": L, "H": H},
     "materials": {"water": {"density": 998.2, "fluid": {"mu_Pa_s": 0.001}}},
     "regions": [{"name": "channel", "shape": {"rect": {"x": [0, "L"], "y": [0, "H"]}}, "material": "water"}],
     "boundaries": {"inlet": {"of": "channel", "where": {"x": 0}}, "outlet": {"of": "channel", "where": {"x": "L"}},
                    "walls": {"of": "channel", "except": ["inlet", "outlet"]}},
     "physics": {"flow": {"type": "fluid.incompressible", "options": {"equation": "stokes", "viscous_form": "laplacian"},
                          "boundary_conditions": {"inlet": {"kind": "inlet", "velocity_m_s": ["6*0.01*y*(H-y)/H^2", 0]},
                                                  "outlet": {"kind": "outlet", "pressure_Pa": 0},
                                                  "walls": {"kind": "wall"}}}},
     "mesh": {"size": "H/8"}}
m = axmp.mesh(d)
im = m.instance()
fm = im.fluids_mesh()                       # a fluids.Mesh: a copy of the instance mesh
bcs = [{"attribute": a, "kind": "dirichlet", "value": lambda x, y: (6 * U * y * (H - y) / H**2, 0.0)}
       for a in im.attributes["inlet"]]
bcs += [{"attribute": a, "kind": "do_nothing"} for a in im.attributes["outlet"]]
bcs += [{"attribute": a, "kind": "dirichlet", "value": (0.0, 0.0)} for a in im.attributes["walls"]]
sol = fluids.solve_stokes(fm, nu, bcs=bcs, form="laplacian")    # the Laplacian form admits the developed outflow

fluids_mesh() returns an axionmultiphysics.fluids.Mesh with the instance mesh's vertices, triangles, boundary segments and boundary attributes in the same order, and its nodes when the mesh has them (Mesh.has_nodes: true at geometry order 2, false at geometry order 1, where an advection-dominated heat solve may use supg=True). It is a copy and owns its data. In a build without the fluids module (a wheel from PyPI, the sequential source build) it raises AxionMultiPhysicsError with the code build.requires_fluids; the MPI source build has it.

chem_mesh(order) returns a chem.TriMesh for chem.CurrentDistribution. order is the field order of the current distribution, 1 or 2; the mesh records the instance's geometry_order and its edge_nodes() are the P2 nodes that lie off their chord (on the circle of an annulus, none on straight edges). A mesh that has nodes is never straightened: chem_mesh(1) on one, CurrentDistribution(mesh, order=1) and CurrentDistribution(mesh, order=2, curved=False) on a mesh that records geometry order 2 all raise a ValueError that names the remedy, as does chem.meshes.red_refine of a curved bridge mesh (refine the mesh by a smaller mesh.size). A model whose physics takes a P1 field has its geometry order lowered to 1 by the validation, so its instance mesh has no nodes.

import axionmultiphysics as axmp
from axionmultiphysics import chem

d = {"schema": "axionmultiphysics.design/1", "name": "cell", "symmetry": "planar",
     "materials": {"bath": {"electrolyte": {"kappa_S_m": 1.0}}},
     "regions": [{"name": "bulk", "shape": {"rect": {"x": [0, 0.01], "y": [0, 0.02]}}, "material": "bath"}],
     "boundaries": {"anode": {"of": "bulk", "where": {"x": 0}}, "cathode": {"of": "bulk", "where": {"x": 0.01}}},
     "reactions": {"electrode": {"plate": {"kind": "linear", "i0_A_m2": 10, "E_eq_V": 0.0}}},
     "physics": {"cell": {"type": "electrochem.current_distribution", "options": {"kinetics": "secondary", "order": 2},
                          "boundary_conditions": {
                              "anode": {"kind": "electrode", "reactions": ["plate"], "phi_s_V": 0.05},
                              "cathode": {"kind": "electrode", "reactions": ["plate"], "phi_s_V": 0.0},
                              "remaining": {"kind": "insulation"}}}},
     "mesh": {"size": 0.001}}
m = axmp.mesh(d)
im = m.instance()
cd = chem.CurrentDistribution(m.chem_mesh(), order=2)
cd.set_conductivity({a: 1.0 for a in im.region_attribute.values()})
cd.add_electrode("anode", im.attributes["anode"], primary=True, phi_s=0.05)
cd.add_electrode("cathode", im.attributes["cathode"], primary=True, phi_s=0.0)
print(cd.solve()["converged"])      # the other two sides are insulating by default

The potential of the parallel-plate cell is linear, so the current per metre of depth is kappa * dV * Hc / gap to round-off. The tolerances of the engine tests that run through this bridge (the closed forms of Poiseuille flow, the two-layer flow, Hagen-Poiseuille flow in a pipe, a heat slab and this cell) are recorded per processor model in cpp/tests/data/model/u2/cases/, written by scripts/model_bridge_tolerances.py --record.

docs.title: Orientation and the direction of markers
docs.text: The orientation rules are in named boundaries.
